lessons.title: How macroeconomic models work
lessons.subtitle: Translate assumptions into equations, diagrams and economic mechanisms.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 1 - Module Info and Introduction.pdf

concepts.title: A model is a conditional argument
concepts.explain: A model simplifies reality to isolate a mechanism. Its result depends on its assumptions. Microfoundations connect aggregate outcomes to choices made by households, workers and firms. A different friction or constraint can change the result.
concepts.formula: Assumptions → optimal choices → market equilibrium → prediction
steps: State the question.
Identify the mechanism and assumptions.
Solve choices and market clearing.
Interpret the result within those assumptions.
concepts.increase: Allowing more adjustment, such as flexible wages, can remove an imbalance that persists under fixed wages.
concepts.decrease: Restricting adjustment, such as fixing prices, can make output respond to demand.
concepts.edge: A mathematical solution need not fit the situation if an assumption fails.
concepts.example: A demand increase raises output in a fixed-price model. With flexible prices and fixed productive capacity, the same demand change may instead raise prices.

check.prompt: Why can two models give different answers to one shock?
check.answer: Their assumptions can allow different adjustment mechanisms.

concepts.title: Endogenous and exogenous depend on the model
concepts.explain: An endogenous variable is solved inside the model. An exogenous variable is taken as given. The labels belong to a particular model, not permanently to a variable.
concepts.formula: c = a + b y, with a, b and y given
steps: List the equations.
List the unknowns solved by them.
Treat remaining inputs as exogenous.
concepts.increase: If given income y rises, this consumption rule predicts higher c when b > 0.
concepts.decrease: If given income y falls, c falls when b > 0.
concepts.edge: In a larger model that determines income, y becomes endogenous.
concepts.example: With a = 10, b = 0.6 and y = 100, c = 70. Here c is endogenous; y is an input.

check.prompt: Is the real wage always exogenous?
check.answer: No. A price-taking worker takes it as given, while a labor-market equilibrium model determines it.

concepts.title: Autonomous does not mean zero
concepts.explain: An autonomous component is unexplained by the variables included in a model. It can be positive and can change between scenarios. A slope measures a response to an included variable.
concepts.formula: C = C₀ + cY − br
steps: Hold Y and r fixed.
Change C₀ to isolate an autonomous demand shift.
Change Y or r to move through the existing relationship.
concepts.increase: Higher C₀ raises desired consumption at every Y and r.
concepts.decrease: Lower C₀ lowers desired consumption at every Y and r.
concepts.edge: Autonomous consumption is a model component, not a claim that people can consume indefinitely without resources.
concepts.example: With C₀ = 20, c = 0.5, Y = 100 and br = 10, C = 60. Increasing C₀ to 25 raises C to 65.

check.prompt: Does a higher Y count as higher autonomous consumption?
check.answer: No. It is the income-induced component cY.

concepts.title: Real purchasing power
concepts.explain: Nominal values use money units. Real values divide a nominal amount by the relevant price level. Economic choices in this course depend on real rewards and costs.
concepts.formula: Real wage w = W/P; real balances = M/P
steps: Identify the nominal amount.
Identify the matching price measure.
Divide and compare purchasing power.
concepts.increase: If W rises with P fixed, w rises. If P rises with W fixed, w falls.
concepts.decrease: If W falls with P fixed, w falls. If P falls with W fixed, w rises.
concepts.edge: Equal proportional changes in numerator and denominator leave the real value unchanged.
concepts.example: W = 120 and P = 3 gives w = 40. If both double, w is still 40.

check.prompt: A nominal wage rises 10% and prices rise 10%. What happens to the real wage?
check.answer: It is unchanged because 1.10/1.10 = 1.

concepts.title: Stocks accumulate flows
concepts.explain: A stock is measured at a date; a flow is measured over a time interval. Saving changes wealth, investment changes capital, and a budget deficit adds to debt, subject to valuation and other adjustments.
concepts.formula: Ending stock = beginning stock + net inflow
steps: Check whether the quantity has a time interval.
Separate gross additions from removals.
Reconcile the change in stock.
concepts.increase: Positive net saving increases wealth when there are no valuation changes.
concepts.decrease: Dissaving reduces wealth, through asset sales or increased debt.
concepts.edge: Capital gains can raise wealth without saving. Gross investment can coexist with falling capital if depreciation is larger.
concepts.example: Wealth starts at 100, saving is 8, and assets lose 3 in value. Ending wealth is 105, not 108.

check.prompt: Is an account balance of 500 a flow?
check.answer: No. A balance at a moment is a stock.

concepts.title: Income, saving and net worth
concepts.explain: Income is a flow earned over a period. Saving is the part not consumed. Wealth is assets minus liabilities. Repaying debt with unconsumed income raises net worth just as acquiring an asset does.
concepts.formula: Wealth = assets − liabilities; saving = income − consumption
steps: Calculate total income.
Subtract consumption.
Trace saving into higher assets or lower liabilities.
concepts.increase: Higher income with unchanged consumption raises saving and wealth accumulation.
concepts.decrease: Higher consumption with unchanged income lowers saving; saving becomes negative when consumption exceeds income.
concepts.edge: Borrowing itself does not increase net worth when it raises cash assets and debt equally.
concepts.example: Assets of 200 and debt of 80 imply wealth of 120. Repaying 10 of debt using 10 of existing cash leaves wealth at 120.

check.prompt: Does taking a 20 loan immediately make someone 20 wealthier?
check.answer: No. Their assets and liabilities both rise by 20.

concepts.title: Movement along a curve versus a shift
concepts.explain: A curve records combinations of its axis variables while other determinants are held fixed. An axis-variable change creates movement along it. A change in a held-fixed determinant changes the relationship itself.
concepts.formula: Nd = Nd(w; A, K)
steps: Read both axes.
List variables held fixed.
Classify which variable changed.
concepts.increase: Higher productivity raises labor demand at every real wage, shifting the curve right.
concepts.decrease: Lower productivity lowers labor demand at every real wage, shifting the curve left.
concepts.edge: The same curve can be described as shifting upward or rightward. These are descriptions of one new relationship, not two shocks.
concepts.example: On a graph with w vertical and N horizontal, a lower w moves down the labor-demand curve. Higher A shifts the whole curve.

check.prompt: Why is a higher wage not a labor-demand shift?
check.answer: The wage is an axis variable on that demand curve.

concepts.title: Marginal conditions and constraints
concepts.explain: An interior optimum equates marginal benefit and marginal cost. A first-order condition locates a stationary point, while curvature and feasibility determine whether it is an optimum.
concepts.formula: dπ/dN = MPN − w = 0; d²π/dN² < 0
steps: Write the objective and feasible choices.
Differentiate including all indirect effects.
Check curvature and boundaries.
Translate the condition into economics.
concepts.increase: When marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost, increasing the choice raises the objective locally.
concepts.decrease: When marginal benefit is below marginal cost, reducing the choice raises the objective locally.
concepts.edge: At a boundary, equality need not hold. A desired negative quantity is infeasible when quantities must be nonnegative.
concepts.example: For π = 10N − N² − 4N, dπ/dN = 6 − 2N gives N = 3 and the second derivative is −2.

check.prompt: Does a zero first derivative always prove a maximum?
check.answer: No. Check the second derivative or global shape and feasible boundaries.

lessons.title: Production and the labor market
lessons.subtitle: From production and individual choices to full employment and unemployment.

concepts.title: Output, technology and inputs
concepts.explain: Production combines capital and labor. Technology A scales how effectively they produce. A production graph varies one input while holding the other input and technology fixed.
steps: Choose the input on the horizontal axis.
Hold the other input and A fixed.
Separate a movement along production from a productivity shift.
concepts.increase: More N raises Y at fixed K and A. Higher A raises Y at every N.
concepts.decrease: Less N lowers Y at fixed K and A. Lower A shifts production down.
concepts.edge: Positive marginal products do not mean output rises at an increasing rate.
concepts.example: With A = 1, α = 0.5 and K = 100, Y = 10√N. Increasing N from 25 to 36 raises Y from 50 to 60.

check.prompt: What must be held fixed when reading MPN from a production graph?
check.answer: Capital and technology.

concepts.title: Diminishing marginal products
concepts.explain: Each marginal product is the partial derivative of output. With the other input fixed, adding an input raises output but reduces the extra output from another unit of the same input.
concepts.formula: MPN = (1−α)Y/N; MPK = αY/K
steps: Differentiate Y with respect to one input.
Differentiate again to assess curvature.
Keep the other input fixed in both steps.
concepts.increase: Higher N raises total Y but lowers MPN. Higher K raises Y but lowers MPK.
concepts.decrease: Lower N reduces Y but raises MPN. Lower K reduces Y but raises MPK.
concepts.edge: Diminishing marginal product is not negative marginal product. Output still rises with the input.
concepts.example: For Y = 10√N, MPN = 5/√N. At N = 25, MPN = 1; at N = 100, MPN = 0.5.

check.prompt: Can output rise while MPN falls?
check.answer: Yes. Output rises more slowly as labor increases.

concepts.title: Capital and labor can raise each other’s productivity
concepts.explain: Cobb–Douglas capital and labor have positive cross partials. More equipment increases the productivity of a given worker; more workers increase the productivity of a given unit of capital.
concepts.formula: ∂MPN/∂K = ∂MPK/∂N = α(1−α)Y/(KN) > 0
steps: Differentiate MPN with respect to K.
Keep N and A fixed.
Distinguish this cross effect from diminishing own marginal product.
concepts.increase: Higher K shifts MPN upward and labor demand right.
concepts.decrease: Lower K shifts MPN downward and labor demand left.
concepts.edge: Positive cross partials are properties of this production specification, not a theorem for every imaginable technology.
concepts.example: With Y = √(KN), doubling K at fixed N multiplies MPN by √2.

check.prompt: Why can MPK fall with K while MPN rises with K?
check.answer: One is an own derivative, the other a cross derivative.

concepts.title: Productivity shocks
concepts.explain: A changes output and marginal products at fixed input quantities. A supply shock affects what can be produced, which then changes firms’ willingness to hire.
concepts.formula: ∂Y/∂A = Y/A; ∂MPN/∂A = MPN/A
steps: Start with A at unchanged K and N.
Trace the rise or fall in MPN.
Then allow firms to adjust hiring.
concepts.increase: A beneficial shock raises output and MPN at every N and increases labor demand.
concepts.decrease: An adverse shock lowers output and MPN at every N and reduces labor demand.
concepts.edge: The initial output effect at fixed N differs from the final effect after labor adjusts.
concepts.example: A 10% increase in A increases Y and MPN by 10% at fixed inputs.

check.prompt: Does lower A move the economy along the original production function?
check.answer: No. The production function itself shifts down.

concepts.title: Returns to scale versus diminishing returns
concepts.explain: Returns to scale changes all inputs together. Diminishing marginal products changes one input while holding the other fixed. Constant returns and diminishing marginal products can therefore coexist.
concepts.formula: F(zK,zN) = z^(α+β)F(K,N)
steps: Add the exponents in a Cobb–Douglas specification.
Compare their sum with one.
Use own derivatives for marginal returns instead.
concepts.increase: Scaling both inputs up by z doubles output when z = 2 and the exponents sum to one.
concepts.decrease: Halving both inputs halves output under constant returns.
concepts.edge: Exponents below one individually do not imply decreasing returns to scale. Their sum matters.
concepts.example: Y = K^0.6N^0.4 has constant returns. Y = K^0.6N^0.6 has increasing returns despite diminishing own marginal products.

check.prompt: What happens to Y = K^0.3N^0.7 when both inputs triple?
check.answer: Output triples.

concepts.title: Factor payments under Cobb–Douglas
concepts.explain: If each factor is paid its marginal product, multiplying marginal product by quantity gives its income. Under constant returns, these factor payments exhaust output.
concepts.formula: MPK·K/Y = α; MPN·N/Y = 1−α
steps: Compute each marginal product.
Multiply by its factor quantity.
Divide by Y to obtain a share.
concepts.increase: Higher Y with unchanged α raises both factor incomes proportionally.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y with unchanged α reduces both factor incomes proportionally.
concepts.edge: These shares rely on marginal-product pricing and the specified technology. Fixed capital is not free capital.
concepts.example: If α = 0.35 and Y = 200, capital receives 70 and labor receives 130.

check.prompt: Does a larger capital stock necessarily increase the capital income share in this specification?
check.answer: No. With unchanged α and marginal-product pricing, the share remains α.

concepts.title: Hiring equates real wage and marginal product
concepts.explain: A competitive firm takes w as given and chooses N. An extra worker adds MPN output and costs w output units. Diminishing MPN makes the interior first-order condition a maximum.
concepts.formula: max π = AF(K,N) − wN; AFN = w
steps: Compare MPN with w.
Hire more if MPN > w.
Hire less if MPN < w.
Stop at equality when feasible.
concepts.increase: A higher real wage lowers optimal hiring along the demand curve.
concepts.decrease: A lower real wage raises optimal hiring along the demand curve.
concepts.edge: At a nonnegative-employment boundary, a firm may hire zero without an interior equality.
concepts.example: For Y = 10√N and w = 1, 5/√N = 1 gives N = 25.

check.prompt: Why does the firm not maximize total output?
check.answer: Additional output can cost more in wages than it is worth.

concepts.title: Deriving labor demand and its sensitivities
concepts.explain: Solve the marginal-product equation for N, then differentiate the demand function. This exposes how technology, capital and wages affect hiring.
steps: Set (1−α)AK^αN^(−α) = w.
Rearrange N^α = (1−α)AK^α/w.
Raise both sides to 1/α.
concepts.increase: Higher A or K raises Nd at every w. A higher w reduces Nd.
concepts.decrease: Lower A or K reduces Nd at every w. A lower w raises Nd.
concepts.edge: The wage elasticity is −1/α, not −α. Parameters must satisfy A, K, w > 0.
concepts.example: With α = 0.5, K = 100, A = 1 and w = 1, Nd = 25. Doubling w reduces Nd to 6.25.

check.prompt: If α = 0.25, what is the labor-demand wage elasticity?

concepts.title: Comparative statics without a functional form
concepts.explain: The implicit-function rule derives response signs from the first-order condition. It does not require solving N explicitly. Local results require a nonzero derivative with respect to N.
concepts.formula: AFN − w = 0; dN/dw = 1/(AFNN); dN/dA = −FN/(AFNN)
steps: Totally differentiate the equilibrium condition.
Hold the other inputs fixed.
Isolate the response derivative.
Use FN > 0 and FNN < 0.
concepts.increase: Higher A increases Nd because −FN/(AFNN) > 0.
concepts.decrease: Lower A reduces Nd; a higher wage reduces Nd since 1/(AFNN) < 0.
concepts.edge: If FNN = 0, this local formula divides by zero and a regular interior demand curve may fail.
concepts.example: For F = √N and A = 10, AFNN = −2.5N^(−3/2), so dN/dw is negative.

check.prompt: What assumption gives downward-sloping labor demand here?
check.answer: Diminishing marginal product of labor, FNN < 0.

concepts.title: The income–leisure budget
concepts.explain: Time is allocated to work or leisure. Each hour of leisure costs the real wage in forgone consumption. Nonlabor income shifts resources without changing this opportunity cost.
concepts.formula: n = h − l; c = w(h−l)+m; c+wl = wh+m
steps: Write total time h.
Subtract leisure to obtain work.
Multiply work by w and add m.
Impose 0 ≤ l ≤ h.
concepts.increase: Higher m shifts the budget line upward by the same amount at every l. Higher w rotates it around (h,m).
concepts.decrease: Lower m shifts the line down. Lower w flattens it around (h,m).
concepts.edge: With m > 0, the algebraic horizontal intercept h+m/w lies beyond feasible leisure h. Do not permit leisure above h.
concepts.example: With h = 16, w = 5 and m = 20, c = 100−5l and the no-work point is (16,20).

check.prompt: Why is the no-work point unchanged when w changes?
check.answer: At l = h there are no paid hours, so c = m.

concepts.title: Why MRS equals the real wage
concepts.explain: A little more leisure directly raises utility but reduces consumption through forgone earnings. The chain rule must include both effects. At an interior optimum they balance.
concepts.formula: −w uc(c,l)+ul(c,l)=0; ul/uc=w
steps: Substitute c = w(h−l)+m into utility.
Differentiate the direct leisure effect and indirect consumption effect.
Set their sum to zero.
concepts.increase: If ul/uc > w at a feasible interior point, more leisure gives greater benefit than cost.
concepts.decrease: If ul/uc < w, reducing leisure and working more raises utility locally.
concepts.edge: A no-work or maximum-work corner needs an inequality condition rather than automatic tangency.
concepts.example: For u = ln c + ln l, ul/uc = c/l. At w = 5, an interior optimum has c = 5l.

check.prompt: Why is ul − wuc the derivative, rather than just ul?
check.answer: Changing leisure also changes the consumption financed by work.

concepts.title: Wealth effects on work
concepts.explain: With normal consumption and leisure, more nonlabor income raises both consumption and leisure. Labor supply falls because leisure uses some of the fixed time endowment.
concepts.formula: dn/dm = −dl/dm < 0 when leisure is normal
steps: Shift the budget line without changing its slope.
Move to higher normal-good consumption and leisure.
Convert higher l into lower n.
concepts.increase: Higher m raises leisure and reduces labor supplied at each w.
concepts.decrease: Lower m reduces leisure and increases labor supplied at each w.
concepts.edge: At the no-work corner, additional income cannot reduce work below zero.
concepts.example: With u = ln c+ln l, h = 16 and w = 5, m = 0 gives l = 8. m = 20 gives l = 10 and work falls from 8 to 6.

check.prompt: Does higher nonlabor income cause a movement along a labor-supply curve?
check.answer: No. It shifts labor supply because w is unchanged.

concepts.title: A wage change has two opposing effects
concepts.explain: A higher wage makes leisure more expensive, encouraging work through substitution. It also expands purchasing power for a worker, encouraging normal leisure through income. The net effect is not fixed by normality alone.
concepts.formula: Δn = substitution effect + income effect
steps: Compensate the wage change to isolate substitution.
Then remove compensation to obtain the income effect.
Compare magnitudes before assigning the net sign.
concepts.increase: A wage rise raises work through substitution and reduces it through income. Work rises only if substitution dominates.
concepts.decrease: A wage fall reduces work through substitution and increases it through the adverse income effect. The net depends on magnitudes.
concepts.edge: Exact cancellation leaves work unchanged. Income dominance gives a backward-bending individual supply segment.
concepts.example: If substitution adds 3 hours and income subtracts 3 hours, hours do not change even though the wage rises.

check.prompt: Does leisure being normal prove upward-sloping individual labor supply?
check.answer: No. Normality determines the income effect, not which effect dominates.

concepts.title: Individual and aggregate labor supply
concepts.explain: Aggregate supply sums work across people. The course usually assumes aggregate labor supply slopes upward, while individual wage responses can be ambiguous. Population, wealth and expected future wages shift supply.
concepts.formula: Ns(w) = sum of individual ni(w)
steps: Separate a wage movement from nonwage determinants.
Add labor supplied across workers.
State the aggregate slope assumption.
concepts.increase: More working-age people or lower household wealth shifts aggregate supply right.
concepts.decrease: Fewer potential workers or higher wealth shifts aggregate supply left.
concepts.edge: A positive aggregate slope does not require every individual to work more after a wage rise.
concepts.example: If 100 workers each supply 8 hours, total labor is 800 hours. Adding 10 identical workers increases supply to 880 at that wage.

check.prompt: Can aggregate supply rise when one worker reduces hours?
check.answer: Yes. Other workers or participation changes can outweigh that response.

concepts.title: Full employment is a market-clearing outcome
concepts.explain: The competitive labor-market intersection determines the real wage and full-employment labor. Substituting this labor into production determines potential output. Full employment is not everyone working all the time.
concepts.formula: Nd(w*) = Ns(w*); Y* = AF(K,N*)
steps: Find the wage clearing labor demand and supply.
Read equilibrium N*.
Insert N* into the production function.
concepts.increase: A demand increase with upward supply raises w*, N* and Y*.
concepts.decrease: A demand decrease with upward supply lowers w*, N* and Y*.
concepts.edge: In the basic competitive model full employment can coexist with frictional and structural unemployment in the wider economy.
concepts.example: If Nd = 100−5w and Ns = 10w, w* = 20/3 and N* = 200/3.

check.prompt: Is Y* determined by arbitrary desired spending in this labor-market calculation?
check.answer: No. It follows from technology, capital and equilibrium employment.

concepts.title: Supply shifts and adverse energy shocks
concepts.explain: Immigration can increase labor supply, while depleted energy reduces productivity. Trace the curve shift and then output, keeping the other determinants fixed.
concepts.formula: Y* = AF(K,N*); MPN = w*
steps: Identify whether the first effect is on labor supply or demand.
Solve the new intersection.
Combine changed employment and technology in production.
concepts.increase: Immigration shifts supply right, lowers the real wage and raises employment and total output under the maintained model.
concepts.decrease: Energy depletion lowers A, shifts demand left and lowers the real wage, employment and output with unchanged supply.
concepts.edge: More total output does not prove higher output per person or that every resident benefits.
concepts.example: Immigration and a productivity improvement can both raise employment, but their wage predictions differ.

check.prompt: What distinguishes an immigration shock from higher productivity in the labor diagram?
check.answer: The former initially shifts supply, the latter demand.

concepts.title: Employment, participation and unemployment
concepts.explain: The unemployed are without work and actively seeking it. People neither employed nor searching are outside the labor force. Unemployment and participation use different denominators.
concepts.formula: Labor force L = E+U; u=U/L; participation=L/adult population
steps: Classify employed, unemployed and outside the labor force.
Construct L.
Use the correct denominator for each rate.
concepts.increase: More unsuccessful active jobseekers increases U and normally raises u. More entrants also raises participation.
concepts.decrease: When an unemployed person stops searching, U and L both fall and u can fall without any new job.
concepts.edge: Discouragement can improve the unemployment rate while employment is unchanged.
concepts.example: If E = 90, U = 10 and adults = 125, u = 10% and participation = 80%.

check.prompt: Is a full-time student who neither works nor seeks work unemployed?
check.answer: No. They are outside the labor force under this classification.

concepts.title: Natural unemployment and Okun’s law
concepts.explain: Natural unemployment includes frictional and structural components. Cyclical unemployment is the difference between actual and natural unemployment. Okun’s law is an empirical relationship, not an accounting identity.
concepts.formula: u cyclical = u−u*; GDP growth ≈ 3% − 2Δu in percentage points
steps: Distinguish level u from change Δu.
Measure the change in percentage points.
Apply the stated coefficient and normal-growth intercept.
concepts.increase: A one percentage point rise in u reduces predicted GDP growth by two percentage points relative to 3%, giving 1%.
concepts.decrease: A one percentage point fall in u raises predicted GDP growth to 5%.
concepts.edge: Unchanged unemployment predicts normal growth of 3%, not zero growth. The numbers are the lecture calibration, not universal constants.
concepts.example: If u rises from 4% to 6%, Δu = 2 percentage points and predicted GDP growth is −1%.

check.prompt: Can natural unemployment be positive at full employment?
check.answer: Yes. Frictional and structural unemployment can remain.

lessons.title: Consumption and saving across time
lessons.subtitle: Solve the lifetime trade-off, then distinguish income, wealth and interest-rate shocks.

concepts.title: Private, public and national saving
concepts.explain: Private saving is disposable income not consumed. Public saving is taxes less government purchases. Combining them cancels taxes directly, although taxes can still affect consumption behavior.
concepts.formula: Sp=Y−T−C; Sg=T−G; S=Y−C−G
steps: Calculate private and public saving separately.
Add them and cancel T.
Distinguish an accounting cancellation from a behavioral effect.
concepts.increase: Higher Y with C and G fixed increases S. Higher G with Y and C fixed reduces S.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y with C and G fixed reduces S. Lower G with Y and C fixed increases S.
concepts.edge: An increase in T need not leave national saving unchanged if C responds.

check.prompt: Why do taxes disappear from the national saving identity?
check.answer: They transfer resources between the private and public sectors, but may still change consumption decisions.

concepts.title: Goods equilibrium versus accounting
concepts.explain: Actual saving equals actual investment in a closed economy when investment includes unintended inventory changes. Desired saving equals desired investment only at goods-market equilibrium.
concepts.formula: Y = Cd+Id+G ⇔ Sd = Id
steps: Define desired expenditure.
Compare it with actual production.
Use inventory surprises to reconcile actual accounting.
Adjust to equilibrium.
concepts.increase: If production exceeds desired spending, unintended inventories accumulate.
concepts.decrease: If desired spending exceeds production, inventories are run down unexpectedly.
concepts.edge: An identity does not prove all agents achieved their desired choices.
concepts.example: If Y=100, Cd=60, Id=15 and G=20, unintended inventory accumulation is 5.

check.prompt: Can desired saving exceed desired investment even though actual saving equals actual investment?
check.answer: Yes. Unintended inventory investment makes the accounting identity hold.

concepts.title: Why consumption is smoother than income
concepts.explain: A forward-looking household uses borrowing and saving to distribute resources across periods. Diminishing marginal utility creates a gain from avoiding very uneven consumption, subject to prices and patience.
steps: Compare current income with desired consumption.
Borrow or save to transfer resources.
Repay debts or spend accumulated wealth by the terminal date.
concepts.increase: A temporary income increase is spread across current and future consumption under smoothing.
concepts.decrease: A temporary income loss can be cushioned by reducing saving or borrowing.
concepts.edge: Borrowing constraints can prevent smoothing. Smooth consumption is not necessarily equal consumption.
concepts.example: A worker can save during high-income years and dissave in retirement even while choosing a smooth consumption path.

check.prompt: Does consumption smoothing mean c1 must equal c2?
check.answer: No. Equality additionally depends on the interest rate, patience and the utility structure.

concepts.title: Building the intertemporal budget
concepts.explain: Saving transfers current resources to the future. Combining both period budgets yields one lifetime constraint. The simple lecture model allows borrowing and lending at the same real interest rate.
steps: Write s1=y1−c1.
Write c2=y2+(1+r)s1.
Substitute and rearrange.
Check that debt is repaid at the terminal date.
concepts.increase: Higher y1 raises present-value resources one for one.
concepts.decrease: Lower y2 reduces present-value resources by its discounted amount.
concepts.edge: If borrowing and lending rates differ, one straight budget line is no longer valid across both regions.
concepts.example: With y1=100, y2=110 and r=10%, resources are 200. Choosing c1=120 leaves c2=88.

check.prompt: Why is c2 divided by 1+r in the present-value constraint?
check.answer: One unit saved today purchases 1+r future units.

concepts.title: Discounting goods is not discounting utility
concepts.explain: The market rate r converts dated goods into comparable resource units. The preference factor β converts future utility into present utility. They perform different tasks.
steps: Choose the date for valuation.
Discount later resources or compound earlier ones.
Use β only when aggregating utility.
concepts.increase: A higher r lowers the PV of a fixed positive future payment.
concepts.decrease: A lower r raises its PV.
concepts.edge: Negative r above −1 makes the PV of a future payment exceed its face amount.
concepts.example: At r=10%, 121 received in two periods has PV=100.

check.prompt: Should future income be discounted using ρ in the budget constraint?
check.answer: No. Use r for resources and ρ or β for preferences.

concepts.title: The endowment pivot
concepts.explain: On a graph with c1 horizontal and c2 vertical, the slope is −(1+r). The endowment bundle remains feasible at every interest rate in the model without initial assets.
steps: Identify the endowment (y1,y2).
Draw the slope through that point.
Locate borrowing to its right and saving to its left.
concepts.increase: Higher r steepens the line, expanding opportunities for savers and worsening terms for borrowers.
concepts.decrease: Lower r flattens the line, worsening returns to saving and improving borrowing terms.
concepts.edge: The fixed pivot at (y1,y2) presumes a0=0. Initial asset returns can change the resource point.
concepts.example: For endowment (100,100), r=0 gives c2=200−c1. r=0.1 gives c2=210−1.1c1; both pass through (100,100).

check.prompt: Which side of the endowment has positive saving?
check.answer: c1<y1, the left side.

concepts.title: Patience and diminishing marginal utility
concepts.explain: Concave period utility values consumption more when consumption is scarce. β measures the weight on future utility. A higher β means greater patience, whereas a higher ρ means less patience.
steps: Read β as a utility weight.
Read concavity as diminishing marginal utility.
Use both with prices to determine the consumption profile.
concepts.increase: Higher β shifts preferred consumption toward the future at fixed resources and r in the standard model.
concepts.decrease: Lower β shifts preferred consumption toward the present.
concepts.edge: Multiplying the entire utility function by a positive constant changes neither preferences nor choices.
concepts.example: ρ=0.25 implies β=0.8; ρ=0.1 implies β≈0.909. The second consumer is more patient.

check.prompt: Does a higher β mean a higher market return on saving?
check.answer: No. It changes preferences, not the market interest rate.

concepts.title: Deriving the Euler condition
concepts.explain: After substituting the budget constraint, more c1 directly raises current utility but lowers c2 by 1+r. The optimum balances these marginal utility effects.
steps: Write c2=(1+r)(y1−c1)+y2.
Apply the chain rule to u(c1)+βu(c2(c1)).
Combine with the budget constraint.
concepts.increase: If current marginal utility exceeds discounted marginal utility from saving, increase c1 locally.
concepts.decrease: If current marginal utility is smaller, reduce c1 and save more locally.
concepts.edge: A binding borrowing constraint may prevent Euler equality. Do not impose an interior condition at every corner.
concepts.example: With logarithmic utility, 1/c1=β(1+r)/c2, so c2=β(1+r)c1.

check.prompt: Why does the Euler equation include 1+r?
check.answer: Forgoing one current unit finances 1+r future units.

concepts.title: Interest versus impatience
concepts.explain: With the same strictly concave period utility in both periods and an interior optimum, comparing r with ρ determines whether consumption rises, stays constant or falls over time.
concepts.formula: r>ρ ⇒ c2>c1; r=ρ ⇒ c2=c1; r<ρ ⇒ c2<c1
steps: Rewrite β(1+r)=(1+r)/(1+ρ).
Compare marginal utilities.
Reverse the inequality when converting marginal utility into consumption.
concepts.increase: Raising r above ρ makes future consumption exceed current consumption at the optimum.
concepts.decrease: Lowering r below ρ makes current consumption exceed future consumption.
concepts.edge: This compares c1 with c2 at an optimum. It does not by itself establish how c1 changes when r changes.
concepts.example: If r=ρ=0.05 and y1=80, y2=122, constant consumption is (1.05×80+122)/2.05≈100.488.

check.prompt: Does r>ρ imply the person must save rather than borrow?
check.answer: No. Saving also depends on current income relative to c1.

concepts.title: Current and future income have different saving effects
concepts.explain: With normal consumption in both periods and unconstrained smoothing, both incomes raise current consumption. Current income also directly funds saving; future income does not.
concepts.formula: ds1/dy1=1−dc1/dy1>0; ds1/dy2=−dc1/dy2<0
steps: Track the change in lifetime resources.
Allocate the gain or loss across both periods.
Use s1=y1−c1 to obtain the saving effect.
concepts.increase: Higher y1 raises c1, c2 and s1. Higher y2 raises c1 and c2 but reduces s1.
concepts.decrease: Lower y1 lowers c1 and c2 and reduces s1. Lower y2 lowers consumption and raises s1.
concepts.edge: The result assumes 0<MPC out of current income<1. A constrained household can consume the entire current gain.
concepts.example: If current income rises 10 and MPC=0.6, c1 rises 6 and saving rises 4. A future-income gain raising c1 by 6 reduces saving by 6.

check.prompt: Why do equal signs for current consumption coexist with opposite signs for saving?
check.answer: Only the current-income change directly changes y1 in s1=y1−c1.

concepts.title: Interest changes are not one universal arrow
concepts.explain: For a saver, higher r creates a favorable income effect and a substitution effect away from current consumption. These oppose for c1. For a borrower, higher r reduces purchasing power and makes c1 relatively expensive.
concepts.formula: Higher r raises the relative price of c1 to c2
steps: Identify whether the household initially saves or borrows.
Separate the compensated substitution effect.
Add the income effect.
Avoid an unconditional saver-consumption prediction.
concepts.increase: For a saver, higher r makes c1 ambiguous and raises c2 under normality. For a borrower, both effects lower c1.
concepts.decrease: For a saver, lower r makes c1 ambiguous and lowers c2. For a borrower, both effects raise c1.
concepts.edge: A finite shock may change borrowing status. The course separately assumes aggregate C falls and desired S rises with r.
concepts.example: A saver facing a higher return may save less to fund a target or save more because future consumption is cheaper. The net requires preferences.

check.prompt: Why is upward-sloping aggregate saving an extra maintained assumption?
check.answer: Individual saver income and substitution effects do not prove it for every household.

concepts.title: Initial wealth earns interest before period 1 consumption
concepts.explain: The supplement dates a0 at the beginning of period 1. It earns r before c1 is chosen. Saving is the change in wealth, not simply the level of assets carried forward.
steps: Compound a0 into period 1.
Add y1 and subtract c1 to obtain a1.
Subtract a0 to obtain saving.
Impose terminal a2=0.
concepts.increase: Higher a0 expands lifetime resources by (1+r) per unit at fixed r.
concepts.decrease: Lower a0 contracts lifetime resources and can lower consumption in both periods.
concepts.edge: Positive a1 can coexist with negative saving if a1<a0. The direction of saving after a wealth change must include the interest-income term.
concepts.example: With a0=100, r=0.1, y1=50 and c1=80, a1=80 and s1=−20, although end-period wealth is positive.

check.prompt: Why is s1 not equal to a1 when initial wealth is positive?
check.answer: Saving measures the change from a0, so s1=a1−a0.

concepts.title: Solving logarithmic and square-root cases
concepts.explain: A functional form turns the Euler equation into a consumption ratio. Combine that ratio with the lifetime budget. Square-root utility has a different ratio from log utility.
concepts.formula: Log u ⇒ c2=β(1+r)c1; square root u ⇒ c2=[β(1+r)]²c1
steps: Differentiate the stated utility.
Solve Euler for c2/c1.
Insert the ratio into c1+c2/(1+r)=Ω.
Compute saving using the appropriate income definition.
concepts.increase: For log utility at fixed r and β, higher Ω raises c1=Ω/(1+β).
concepts.decrease: Lower Ω reduces c1 and c2 in the same proportion for these homothetic examples.
concepts.edge: Do not reuse a formula from a different utility function. At r=ρ both cases give c1=c2.
concepts.example: For square-root utility, c1=Ω/[1+β²(1+r)]. With β=0.8, r=0.25 and Ω=180, c1=100 and c2=100.

check.prompt: What is the square-root c2/c1 ratio when β=0.9 and r=0.2?

concepts.title: Check feasibility before declaring an optimum
concepts.explain: An unconstrained solution assumes borrowing and lending are available and all dated resources can be traded at r. A borrowing limit may prevent the desired transfer, making current income especially important.
concepts.formula: No borrowing with a0=0 implies s1≥0 and c1≤y1
steps: Solve the unconstrained problem.
Check c1 against the borrowing limit.
If it violates the limit, consider the boundary.
Recheck future consumption and utility.
concepts.increase: A current income increase can relax a binding borrowing limit and permit higher c1.
concepts.decrease: A current income fall can tighten the limit and force a larger consumption drop.
concepts.edge: An expected future windfall may not raise c1 when borrowing is prohibited and the constraint remains binding.
concepts.example: If desired c1=120 but y1=80 and borrowing is forbidden, c1 cannot exceed 80 in the simple endowment model.

check.prompt: Should the Euler equality be used to justify c1=120 here?
check.answer: No. The candidate violates the constraint.

lessons.title: Working and saving over a lifetime
lessons.subtitle: Combine consumption timing with the choice of when to work.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 1.pdf

concepts.title: Labor income becomes endogenous
concepts.explain: Replacing endowment income with wage times chosen hours links consumption to work. Wages and time endowments are inputs, while hours and earnings are outcomes of the household problem.
concepts.formula: yt=wt(h−lt); nt=h−lt
steps: Choose leisure in each period.
Convert leisure into work.
Calculate labor income.
Finance consumption and saving from that income.
concepts.increase: More current work raises current income at fixed w1.
concepts.decrease: Less current work lowers current income at fixed w1.
concepts.edge: An increase in w1 need not increase hours because income and substitution effects oppose.
concepts.example: With h=16, l1=10 and w1=4, n1=6 and y1=24.

check.prompt: Is y1 still exogenous after this substitution?
check.answer: No. It depends on the chosen leisure l1.

concepts.title: One lifetime budget for four goods
concepts.explain: Current consumption, future consumption and leisure in both periods compete for lifetime resources. Leisure has an opportunity cost equal to the wage earned by working instead.
steps: Write s1=w1(h−l1)−c1.
Write c2=w2(h−l2)+(1+r)s1.
Eliminate s1.
Keep the time bounds in both periods.
concepts.increase: Higher w1 or w2 expands earning opportunities at fixed leisure.
concepts.decrease: Lower w1 or w2 contracts earning opportunities at fixed leisure.
concepts.edge: The household need not choose the same leisure in both periods even if h is the same.
concepts.example: With h=10, l1=l2=5, w1=2, w2=3 and r=0, lifetime consumption totals 25.

check.prompt: Does the model allow c1 to exceed current labor income?
check.answer: Yes, if borrowing is allowed and future resources repay the debt.

concepts.title: Three independent choices after substitution
concepts.explain: There are four consumption/leisure quantities but one binding lifetime budget. After solving for c2, the independent choices are c1, l1 and l2. c2 still changes optimally through those choices.
steps: Solve the budget for c2.
Substitute it into lifetime utility.
Differentiate with respect to c1, l1 and l2.
Recover c2 from the budget.
concepts.increase: Increasing c1 by one reduces c2 by 1+r. Increasing l1 by one reduces c2 by (1+r)w1.
concepts.decrease: Reducing l2 by one frees w2 future consumption units. Reducing l1 frees (1+r)w1 future units.
concepts.edge: Not treating c2 as an independent variable after substitution does not mean the household has no preference over it.
concepts.example: If w1=4, w2=6 and r=0.25, the three derivatives are −1.25, −5 and −6.

check.prompt: Why would independently choosing c2 as well overcount freedom?
check.answer: The lifetime budget has already determined c2 from the other three choices.

concepts.title: Consumption Euler condition with leisure
concepts.explain: The intertemporal condition still compares marginal consumption utility across dates. Here each marginal utility is evaluated at both consumption and leisure in its period.
concepts.formula: uc(c1,l1)=β(1+r)uc(c2,l2)
steps: Differentiate current consumption utility.
Include c1’s effect on c2.
Balance the marginal utilities at an interior optimum.
concepts.increase: If the current marginal utility exceeds β(1+r) times future marginal utility, raise c1 locally.
concepts.decrease: If it is lower, reduce c1 and transfer resources forward.
concepts.edge: For nonseparable u(c,l), r=ρ equates uc across periods but does not alone guarantee c1=c2 if leisure differs.
concepts.example: With u=ln c+ln l, uc=1/c and c2=β(1+r)c1. Leisure does not enter uc in this separable example.

check.prompt: What changes relative to the endowment Euler condition?
check.answer: The marginal utilities may now depend on leisure as well as consumption.

concepts.title: Two within-period leisure conditions
concepts.explain: Each period has its own consumption–leisure trade-off. Combining the c1 and l1 FOCs cancels the future marginal-utility term and gives the familiar MRS condition.
concepts.formula: ul(c1,l1)/uc(c1,l1)=w1; ul(c2,l2)/uc(c2,l2)=w2
steps: For l1, differentiate direct leisure and indirect future consumption.
Use the Euler condition to simplify.
For l2, both effects occur in period 2, so β cancels.
concepts.increase: If a period’s leisure MRS exceeds its wage, increase leisure locally.
concepts.decrease: If its leisure MRS is below its wage, work more locally.
concepts.edge: The future within-period condition is MRS=w2, not βw2 or (1+r)w2.
concepts.example: For u=ln c+ln l, c1=w1l1 and c2=w2l2 at an interior optimum.

check.prompt: Why is there no β in the future within-period MRS condition?
check.answer: Both future marginal utilities receive the same β weight.

concepts.title: The price of leisure across time
concepts.explain: An hour of leisure today sacrifices w1 current goods, which could grow to (1+r)w1 future goods. An hour of future leisure sacrifices w2 future goods. Their ratio governs substitution between dates.
concepts.formula: Relative price of l1 to l2 = (1+r)w1/w2
steps: Value both forgone earnings at the same date.
Divide current leisure’s future-valued cost by future leisure’s cost.
Use the ratio to interpret the substitution effect.
concepts.increase: Higher w1 raises the relative price of current leisure and encourages work now through substitution.
concepts.decrease: Higher w2 lowers the relative price of current leisure and encourages work later through substitution.
concepts.edge: The relative-price effect alone omits the wealth effect of higher wages.
concepts.example: With w1=10, w2=15 and r=0.2, the ratio is 0.8. An hour of current leisure costs 0.8 hours of future leisure.

check.prompt: Why is w1/w2 insufficient when r is nonzero?
check.answer: Current forgone earnings could earn interest before period 2.

concepts.title: A current wage shock has opposing effects
concepts.explain: A higher current wage makes current leisure expensive relative to consumption and future leisure. It also makes the worker wealthier. With normal leisure, these substitution and income effects conflict.
concepts.formula: Higher w1 → substitution raises n1; income lowers n1
steps: Hold w2 and r fixed.
Trace the relative-price substitution effect.
Trace the lifetime-income effect.
Compare magnitudes.
concepts.increase: A rise in w1 increases n1 if substitution dominates, reduces n1 if income dominates, and leaves it unchanged under cancellation.
concepts.decrease: A fall in w1 reduces n1 through substitution but raises it through the negative income effect. The net remains conditional.
concepts.edge: An upward-sloping current labor-supply curve assumes substitution dominates; it is not a consequence of normal leisure alone.
concepts.example: A temporary wage bonus can encourage extra hours, but a sufficiently strong wealth effect can lead the worker to take more leisure.

check.prompt: Is the response to w1 a shift of the current labor-supply curve?
check.answer: No. w1 is the axis variable, so this is movement along the curve.

concepts.title: A future wage shock changes current work
concepts.explain: In the tutorial’s maintained normal-good and substitution framework, higher future wages make future leisure expensive relative to current leisure and increase lifetime wealth. Both effects raise current leisure.
concepts.formula: Higher w2 → lower n1; lower w2 → higher n1
steps: Hold current w1 fixed.
Compare the intertemporal relative wage.
Add the current leisure income effect.
Classify the current labor-supply shift.
concepts.increase: Higher w2 encourages shifting work toward the future and consuming more leisure today. Current labor supply shifts left.
concepts.decrease: Lower w2 encourages work today relative to tomorrow and reduces lifetime wealth. Both effects increase current work, shifting supply right.
concepts.edge: A binding borrowing limit or unavailable future work can prevent the course mechanism. Do not extend the conclusion mechanically to those cases.
concepts.example: A credible expected rise in future earning power can reduce current part-time work even though today’s wage is unchanged.

check.prompt: Why is the current work response clearer for w2 than for w1?
check.answer: For w2 the two effects on current leisure reinforce; for w1 they oppose.

lessons.title: Government spending and tax timing
lessons.subtitle: Follow the resources across both periods before predicting consumption.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 2.pdf

concepts.title: The government must finance its purchases
concepts.explain: Borrowing transfers financing across dates. With no inherited debt and no terminal debt, spending and taxes have equal present values. All amounts here are real.
concepts.formula: B₁ = G₁ − T₁; G₂ + (1+r)B₁ = T₂; G₁ + G₂/(1+r) = T₁ + T₂/(1+r)
steps: Write the current deficit.
Carry debt and interest into period 2.
Eliminate debt to obtain the present-value constraint.
concepts.increase: Higher G₁ with unchanged T₁ and G₂ raises borrowing and requires higher T₂.
concepts.decrease: Lower G₁ under the same conditions reduces borrowing and required future taxes.
concepts.edge: A surplus means B₁ < 0. Government saving earns interest and can finance future purchases.
concepts.example: With G₁=100, T₁=80, G₂=50 and r=0.10, B₁=20 and T₂=72.

check.prompt: Can unchanged future spending and taxes finance an extra current purchase forever?
check.answer: No. The terminal budget condition rules out unpaid debt in this two-period model.

concepts.title: Lump-sum taxes change wealth, not relative prices
concepts.explain: A lump-sum tax does not depend on work, consumption or any chosen action. It reduces resources without directly changing the relative price of leisure or dated consumption.
concepts.formula: PVLR = y₁ + y₂/(1+r) − t₁ − t₂/(1+r)
steps: Identify what the tax depends on.
Subtract its present value from resources.
Use the unchanged budget-line slope for the substitution comparison.
concepts.increase: An uncompensated increase in a lump-sum tax reduces lifetime wealth and normally reduces both dates of consumption.
concepts.decrease: An uncompensated decrease raises lifetime wealth and normally raises both dates of consumption.
concepts.edge: A tax proportional to earnings changes the net wage and therefore has a substitution effect. Do not label it lump-sum.
concepts.example: A fixed tax of 40 applies even if hours change. A 20% earnings tax does not.

check.prompt: Does a lump-sum tax have no effects at all?
check.answer: No. It has a wealth or income effect even though it has no direct substitution effect.

concepts.title: Temporary spending and consumption smoothing
concepts.explain: At fixed output and interest rate, an extra temporary government purchase must be financed by taxes. Consumers spread the wealth loss over time, so current consumption typically falls by less than the increase in G.
concepts.formula: Sᵈ = Y − Cᵈ − G; ΔSᵈ = −ΔCᵈ − ΔG when Y is fixed
steps: Find the added lifetime tax burden.
Spread the consumption reduction across periods.
Subtract government purchases and consumption from output.
concepts.increase: A temporary rise in G reduces C today but, under smoothing, reduces national saving because the direct G effect is larger.
concepts.decrease: A temporary fall in G raises C today but raises national saving because the released resources exceed the extra current consumption.
concepts.edge: The result uses normal consumption at both dates and a temporary purchase change. A different spending path can change how the burden is shared.
concepts.example: If ΔG=100 and ΔC=−45 at fixed Y, then ΔS=−55.

check.prompt: Why does lower consumption not imply higher saving after higher G?
check.answer: National saving also subtracts G. Its increase can exceed the fall in C.

concepts.title: Ricardian equivalence is a tax-timing result
concepts.explain: For a fixed government spending path, changing the timing of lump-sum taxes leaves the present value of taxes unchanged. Unconstrained forward-looking households with the relevant tax horizon can keep consumption unchanged.
concepts.formula: ΔT₂ = −(1+r)ΔT₁ when ΔG₁=ΔG₂=0
steps: Hold government spending fixed.
Use the government constraint to infer the future tax offset.
Check that household after-tax lifetime wealth is unchanged.
concepts.increase: A current tax cut increases disposable income, but the matching future liability induces equal extra private saving.
concepts.decrease: A current tax increase reduces disposable income, but the matching future tax cut induces lower private saving.
concepts.edge: The proposition does not say government purchases never matter. It concerns deficit changes caused entirely by tax timing.
concepts.example: At r=5%, a current cut of 200 requires a future increase of 210. Its present value is 200.

check.prompt: Why must the future tax offset exceed the current tax cut when r>0?
check.answer: The government must repay interest as well as principal.

concepts.title: Private and public saving move separately
concepts.explain: National saving combines private saving and government saving. Under Ricardian equivalence, a tax-timing change moves the two components in opposite directions without changing their sum.
concepts.formula: Sprivate = Y − T − C; Sgovernment = T − G; Snational = Y − C − G
steps: Calculate private saving after taxes.
Calculate the government surplus.
Add them and cancel taxes.
concepts.increase: A tax increase with unchanged C and G raises government saving and lowers private saving equally.
concepts.decrease: A tax cut with unchanged C and G lowers government saving and raises private saving equally.
concepts.edge: Taxes disappear from the accounting formula but can still affect national saving indirectly if they change consumption.
concepts.example: Y=1000,C=600,G=200,T=150 gives private saving 250, government saving−50, national saving 200.

check.prompt: If T falls by 50 and C rises by 20 at fixed Y and G, what happens to national saving?
check.answer: It falls by 20. Private saving rises 30 while government saving falls 50.

concepts.title: A borrowing limit can make timing matter
concepts.explain: A household can wish to borrow against future income but be unable to do so. A current tax cut may relax the binding limit, allowing higher current consumption despite unchanged lifetime resources.
concepts.formula: c₁ ≤ y₁ − t₁ when borrowing is prohibited and initial wealth is zero
steps: Find the unconstrained desired borrowing.
Compare it with the borrowing limit.
Test whether the current tax change relaxes that binding constraint.
concepts.increase: More current tax relief can raise current consumption for a constrained household, with some cost borne through future consumption.
concepts.decrease: Higher current taxes can reduce current consumption sharply when the household cannot borrow.
concepts.edge: If the household was already saving, a no-borrowing constraint is not binding. Its existence alone does not establish failure of equivalence.
concepts.example: A household at c₁=y₁−t₁=80 can consume 100 after a current tax cut 20 if its desired consumption remains above 100.

check.prompt: Does every household with low income violate Ricardian equivalence?
check.answer: No. What matters is whether the financing constraint binds, together with the other assumptions.

concepts.title: Whose future taxes count?
concepts.explain: A household must internalize the relevant future tax burden for tax timing to be neutral. Concern for descendants can extend the effective planning horizon through bequests, but this mechanism need not operate for everyone.
concepts.formula: PV of taxes internalized by the household determines its perceived wealth
steps: Identify who pays the later taxes.
Determine whether current households care about those taxpayers.
Check whether bequests can adjust.
concepts.increase: If later taxes fall on descendants and bequests adjust upward, a current tax cut can leave family consumption unchanged.
concepts.decrease: If current taxes rise and future descendants benefit, bequests may fall, preserving consumption when the transfer margin is available.
concepts.edge: Zero intended bequests can create a boundary. Households cannot necessarily offset a current tax rise by making negative bequests.
concepts.example: A parent who fully offsets a future tax burden of 105 at r=5% saves an extra 100 today.

check.prompt: Does finite life alone logically rule out Ricardian equivalence?
check.answer: No. Operative intergenerational transfers can transmit the future liability.

concepts.title: Evidence tests conditions, not an identity
concepts.explain: The withholding example delays tax payments rather than reducing lifetime taxes. Spending responses challenge strict neutrality for some households, but a survey alone cannot identify whether constraints, myopia or another mechanism caused them.
concepts.formula: Tax timing unchanged in present value does not imply observed ΔC must equal zero when assumptions fail
steps: Distinguish permanent relief from delayed payment.
Compare observed plans with the neutrality prediction.
Separate evidence of a response from evidence about its cause.
concepts.increase: A larger current spending response to a temporary withholding reduction is harder to reconcile with universal strict equivalence.
concepts.decrease: A smaller spending response and larger saving or debt repayment response is more consistent with consumption smoothing, without proving all assumptions.
concepts.edge: Survey intentions are not the same as measured spending. A mixture of responses need not imply one representative household describes everyone.
concepts.example: If 40 of 100 households plan to spend the payment, strict neutrality does not describe all reported intentions.

check.prompt: Can spending after a tax delay prove every spender is myopic?
check.answer: No. A binding borrowing constraint can also produce that response.

lessons.title: Capital, investment and the goods market
lessons.subtitle: Separate the desired stock from the flow needed to reach it.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 3.pdf

concepts.title: What counts as investment?
concepts.explain: Macroeconomic investment adds produced capital, housing or inventories. Buying an existing financial claim transfers ownership and is not itself new investment in Y=C+I+G.
concepts.formula: I = business fixed investment + residential investment + inventory investment
steps: Ask whether a produced capital good is added.
Distinguish new production from an ownership transfer.
Count unsold current production in inventories.
concepts.increase: Higher production relative to sales raises inventory investment.
concepts.decrease: Lower production relative to sales reduces inventories and can make inventory investment negative.
concepts.edge: An existing house sale is principally a transfer. Newly produced brokerage services still count in current output.
concepts.example: A firm produces 100 units and sells 92. Inventory investment is 8 units.

check.prompt: Does purchasing a company share automatically add to GDP investment?
check.answer: No. The financial transaction itself is not production of a new capital good.

concepts.title: Capital moves through accumulation and depreciation
concepts.explain: Investment this period becomes productive capital next period. Depreciation reduces the inherited stock even when there is no new investment.
concepts.formula: K₂ = (1−d)K₁ + I₁
steps: Start with inherited capital.
Subtract depreciation.
Add current gross investment to obtain next-period capital.
concepts.increase: More current investment raises next-period capital one for one in this specification.
concepts.decrease: Less current investment lowers next-period capital relative to its former path.
concepts.edge: Zero gross investment does not mean an unchanged stock when d>0. Maintaining capital requires replacement investment.

check.prompt: What investment holds K constant at 80 with depreciation 5%?

concepts.title: Why the firm values future profits
concepts.explain: Choosing capital sacrifices current goods for future output and remaining capital. The firm discounts both future operating profits and the salvage value of undepreciated capital.
concepts.formula: Π = A₁F(K₁,N₁)−w₁N₁−[K₂−(1−d)K₁] + [A₂F(K₂,N₂)−w₂N₂+(1−d)K₂]/(1+r)
steps: Replace investment using capital accumulation.
Include the end-of-period-2 sale of remaining capital.
Discount period-2 proceeds before choosing K₂.
concepts.increase: Higher expected future productivity raises the marginal benefit of current investment.
concepts.decrease: Lower expected future productivity lowers that benefit.
concepts.edge: Omitting salvage changes the capital FOC to MPK₂=1+r. That is a different terminal-value assumption.
concepts.example: With r=.05,d=.10, capital yielding MPK₂=.15 also leaves .90 of salvage. Total payoff 1.05 matches its opportunity cost.

check.prompt: Why is the relevant marginal product future MPK?
check.answer: Current investment becomes capital only in the next period.

concepts.title: The firm has three choice conditions
concepts.explain: The two-period firm chooses N₁, N₂ and K₂. Within each period, labor is hired until its real marginal product equals the real wage. Discounting the future condition multiplies both benefit and wage cost equally.
concepts.formula: MPN₁=w₁; MPN₂=w₂; MPK₂=r+d when pₖ=1
steps: Differentiate profits with respect to each date of labor.
Cancel the positive discount factor from the future labor condition.
Use the capital FOC separately.
concepts.increase: A higher current wage lowers current labor demand along a diminishing-MPN curve.
concepts.decrease: A lower current wage raises current labor demand along that curve.
concepts.edge: A higher interest rate does not insert an extra (1+r) into MPN₂=w₂. Both future revenues and wages are discounted.
concepts.example: A future extra worker produces 6 goods and costs wage 5. Hiring raises PV profits by 1/(1+r).

check.prompt: Must MPN₂ equal (1+r)w₂?
check.answer: No. At an interior optimum MPN₂=w₂.

concepts.title: The user cost is an opportunity cost
concepts.explain: Owning capital for a period incurs foregone real interest and physical depreciation. The lecture formula assumes the same real capital price and abstracts from capital gains.
concepts.formula: uc = (r+d)pₖ
steps: Measure r and d as decimals.
Add financing and depreciation rates.
Multiply by the real price per unit of capital.
concepts.increase: A rise in r increases user cost by pₖΔr and discourages capital holding.
concepts.decrease: A fall in r lowers user cost and encourages capital holding.
concepts.edge: If future capital prices change, expected capital gains matter. The simple formula should not be applied unchanged.
concepts.example: r=.04,d=.08,pₖ=50 gives uc=6 goods per unit per period.

check.prompt: Is pₖ itself the entire one-period cost?
check.answer: No. The remaining capital can be sold, so the cost includes interest and depreciation rather than the full purchase price.

concepts.title: Read the MPK and user-cost intersection
concepts.explain: With diminishing future MPK and constant user cost, the interior optimal stock equates the marginal return and marginal cost. Stocks on either side leave a profitable adjustment.
concepts.formula: MPKᶠ(K*) = uc
steps: Draw a downward-sloping MPK curve.
Draw horizontal user cost.
Compare the marginal benefit and cost on each side.
concepts.increase: If MPK exceeds uc at the current stock, increasing capital raises profit until the gap closes.
concepts.decrease: If MPK is below uc, reducing capital raises profit until equality is restored.
concepts.edge: Equality alone is insufficient without the second-order or diminishing-productivity condition. A physical boundary can also prevent an interior solution.
concepts.example: MPK=12/√K and uc=3 imply √K=4 and K*=16.

check.prompt: Why does a horizontal user-cost line not imply a horizontal investment demand curve?
check.answer: User cost is horizontal against K for a given r. Changing r moves that line and changes K*.

concepts.title: Distinguish a shift from a movement
concepts.explain: Future technology changes the MPK schedule. A real interest-rate change alters user cost and therefore moves the optimum along a given MPK schedule.
concepts.formula: For MPK=A K^(−α), K*=(A/uc)^(1/α), α>0
steps: Identify whether benefit or cost changes.
Find the new intersection.
Translate the desired stock into investment.
concepts.increase: Higher future productivity shifts MPK up and raises K* at a given user cost.
concepts.decrease: Lower future productivity shifts MPK down and lowers K*.
concepts.edge: A change in current productivity alone need not shift future MPK. Its persistence must be specified.
concepts.example: With MPK=A/√K and uc=2, raising A from 8 to 10 raises K* from 16 to 25.

check.prompt: Does higher r shift the technological MPK curve?
check.answer: No. It raises user cost.

concepts.title: Taxes alter the required pre-tax return
concepts.explain: For the lecture revenue-tax example, only a fraction 1−τ of the marginal product is retained. The firm therefore requires a higher pre-tax MPK for the same user cost.
concepts.formula: (1−τ)MPKᶠ = uc; MPKᶠ = uc/(1−τ)
steps: Calculate the retained share.
Divide user cost by that share.
Intersect the higher required return with diminishing MPK.
concepts.increase: A higher revenue or effective tax rate raises the tax-adjusted user cost and lowers K*.
concepts.decrease: A lower rate reduces the required pre-tax MPK and raises K*.
concepts.edge: The expression assumes τ<1 and this particular tax structure. A tax on pure economic profits need not have the same effect.
concepts.example: uc=6 and τ=.25 imply required pre-tax MPK=8.

check.prompt: Is a tax rate increase from 20% to 40% a 20% increase in the required return?
check.answer: No. uc/.6 divided by uc/.8 is 4/3, a 33.3% rise.

concepts.title: Allowances and credits act differently
concepts.explain: A depreciation allowance reduces taxable profit. An investment tax credit directly reduces the tax bill by a share of eligible capital expenditure. Both can lower the effective tax burden on investment.
concepts.formula: Tax saving from a deduction = tax rate × deduction; tax credit reduces tax due directly
steps: Determine whether the provision changes taxable income or tax due.
Compute the monetary tax saving.
Interpret the resulting investment incentive.
concepts.increase: A more generous allowance or credit normally increases the incentive to invest, holding other provisions fixed.
concepts.decrease: A smaller allowance or credit normally reduces that incentive.
concepts.edge: A 100 deduction and a 100 tax credit are not equivalent. Whether deductions can actually be used can matter.
concepts.example: With a 25% tax rate, a 100 deduction saves 25 in tax. A 100 usable credit saves 100.

check.prompt: Why use an effective tax rate?
check.answer: It summarizes the combined investment incentives from the actual tax provisions as an equivalent revenue-tax wedge.

concepts.title: Gross investment is not net investment
concepts.explain: Gross investment contains both expansion and replacement. Even a shrinking desired stock can require positive gross investment if depreciation is sufficiently large.
concepts.formula: I = K*−K + dK; net investment = K*−K
steps: Calculate the desired net change.
Calculate replacement dK.
Add them, keeping their meanings separate.
concepts.increase: A higher desired stock raises gross investment one for one with inherited K and d fixed.
concepts.decrease: A lower desired stock reduces gross investment, which may remain positive.
concepts.edge: A higher depreciation rate both raises replacement needs and reduces K* through user cost. Its total effect on gross investment is not universally signed.
concepts.example: K=100,d=.10,K*=96 gives net investment−4 but gross investment 6.

check.prompt: Does I>0 prove the capital stock rises?
check.answer: No. I must exceed dK.

concepts.title: Desired spending versus the accounting identity
concepts.explain: Actual output equals actual expenditure, including unintended inventory investment. Goods-market equilibrium additionally requires desired saving to equal desired investment.
concepts.formula: Y=Cᵈ+Iᵈ+G ⇔ Sᵈ=Iᵈ, where Sᵈ=Y−Cᵈ−G
steps: Compute desired consumption and investment.
Compare desired expenditure with output.
Use r to reconcile desired saving and investment at fixed Y.
concepts.increase: If desired investment exceeds desired saving, r rises, raising desired saving and reducing desired investment in the maintained model.
concepts.decrease: If desired saving exceeds desired investment, r falls, reducing saving and increasing investment.
concepts.edge: The accounting identity can hold while desired plans fail to match, because unsold goods become unintended inventories.

check.prompt: Does observing actual S=I prove firms wanted their inventory accumulation?
check.answer: No. Actual investment includes unintended inventories.

concepts.title: Crowding out works through the interest rate
concepts.explain: At fixed output, higher government purchases reduce desired national saving, given the consumption response. The real interest rate rises to clear the goods market and discourages investment.
concepts.formula: G↑ → Sᵈ schedule left → r↑ → Iᵈ↓
steps: Hold the output level and other schedules fixed.
Shift desired saving for the fiscal change.
Move along the investment curve to the new equilibrium.
concepts.increase: Higher G typically raises r and lowers equilibrium investment in this fixed-output loanable-funds setup.
concepts.decrease: Lower G typically lowers r and raises equilibrium investment.
concepts.edge: A fiscal expansion in a fixed-price IS–LM model may also raise Y. Do not assume the fixed-output magnitude applies in every model.
concepts.example: If C is independent of r and Y is fixed, extra G displaces I one for one. If C falls with r, both C and I can share the reduction.

check.prompt: Does a tax cut necessarily crowd out investment under Ricardian equivalence?
check.answer: No. A pure Ricardian tax-timing change leaves national saving unchanged.

lessons.title: Money, asset markets and inflation
lessons.subtitle: Keep real balances, nominal returns and expectations distinct.

concepts.title: Money solves an exchange problem
concepts.explain: Money is widely accepted as payment. Its medium-of-exchange role avoids the double coincidence of wants, its unit-of-account role denominates values, and its store-of-value role transfers purchasing power through time.
concepts.formula: Real purchasing power of nominal money = M/P
steps: Identify which function a situation illustrates.
Separate acceptance in exchange from value over time.
Check whether inflation weakens purchasing power.
concepts.increase: A higher P reduces the purchasing power of a fixed nominal balance and weakens its store-of-value performance.
concepts.decrease: A lower P raises its purchasing power.
concepts.edge: An asset can store value without being widely accepted in payment. Being valuable alone does not make it money.
concepts.example: A price tag of 10 dollars uses money as a unit of account. Paying those 10 dollars uses it as a medium of exchange.

check.prompt: Does money have to earn interest to store value?
check.answer: No. It can transfer purchasing power even at zero nominal interest, although inflation can erode it.

concepts.title: Liquidity differs from return and intrinsic value
concepts.explain: Liquidity describes ease and speed of converting an asset into payment. Fiat money has no intrinsic commodity value, while commodity money does. Neither definition ranks every asset by expected return.
concepts.formula: Portfolio choice compares expected return, risk and liquidity
steps: Ask how readily the asset pays for purchases.
Separately assess its expected return and uncertainty.
Avoid equating physical value with monetary usefulness.
concepts.increase: Higher liquidity makes an asset more attractive when return and risk are unchanged.
concepts.decrease: Lower liquidity makes it less attractive under the same comparison.
concepts.edge: An asset may be liquid yet risky. A stable-valued asset may still be costly to sell quickly.
concepts.example: A banknote is fiat money. A cigarette used in a camp has both monetary and consumption uses.

check.prompt: Is the highest-return asset necessarily the most liquid?
check.answer: No. These are separate portfolio characteristics.

concepts.title: Monetary definitions can change measured money
concepts.explain: The lecture distinguishes narrow and broad monetary aggregates and explains the US savings-deposit reclassification. An aggregate can jump because its definition changes even without a corresponding new transaction.
concepts.formula: M2 includes M1 plus specified less-liquid components
steps: Check the definition and date of the series.
Identify whether a change reflects new balances or reclassification.
Compare like definitions before inferring behavior.
concepts.increase: Moving a category into M1 raises measured M1 at the reclassification date.
concepts.decrease: Moving a category out would lower measured M1 even if underlying balances were unchanged.
concepts.edge: The lecture uses revised US definitions. Do not apply the old statement that savings deposits are always outside M1.
concepts.example: Moving 500 of existing savings deposits from an M2-only component into M1 increases M1 by 500 while total M2 is unchanged.

check.prompt: Does a definitional jump in M1 by itself establish a monetary stimulus?
check.answer: No. First separate classification effects from changes in actual assets and policy.

concepts.title: Open-market operations change nominal money
concepts.explain: In the course model the central bank sets nominal M exogenously. Buying existing assets from the public pays out money. Selling assets withdraws money from the public.
concepts.formula: Real supply = M/P
steps: Track what the central bank gives to the public.
Determine the change in nominal money.
Divide by P to obtain real balances.
concepts.increase: An open-market purchase increases M and, at fixed P, increases real money supply.
concepts.decrease: An open-market sale reduces M and real balances at fixed P.
concepts.edge: Directly purchasing new government debt is fiscal financing, distinct from an open-market purchase of existing securities.
concepts.example: M rises from 200 to 220 at P=2, so real supply rises from 100 to 110.

check.prompt: If M and P both rise 10%, do real balances rise?
check.answer: No. Their ratio is unchanged.

concepts.title: Money demand is a desired stock
concepts.explain: Households allocate their wealth among monetary and nonmonetary assets. Money demand means the amount people wish to hold, not their income flow or their desire to earn more money.
concepts.formula: Monetary asset demand + nonmonetary asset demand = wealth
steps: Fix the wealth total.
Compare risk, return and liquidity.
Allocate the stock across asset categories.
concepts.increase: Greater wealth can increase money holdings even if the desired portfolio share is unchanged.
concepts.decrease: Lower wealth can reduce money holdings under the same share rule.
concepts.edge: An individual can try to reduce money holdings by buying bonds, but the community cannot make the fixed nominal money stock disappear through trades among its members.
concepts.example: Wealth 1000 with a 20% money share implies money demand 200.

check.prompt: Can all asset demands independently exceed wealth in a feasible portfolio?
check.answer: No. The portfolio budget restricts their sum.

concepts.title: The nominal return is money’s opportunity cost
concepts.explain: In the baseline model money pays zero nominal interest and bonds pay i. Higher output raises transactions demand, while higher i makes holding money more costly.
concepts.formula: L=L(Y,i), L_Y>0, L_i<0; i≈r+πᵉ
steps: Identify the transaction requirement Y.
Identify the nominal return forgone.
Distinguish real L from nominal demand PL.
concepts.increase: Higher Y raises real money demand. Higher i reduces it, holding the other argument fixed.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y reduces real money demand. Lower i raises it.
concepts.edge: If money itself pays interest iₘ, the relevant opportunity cost is the return gap i−iₘ, rather than i alone.
concepts.example: L=20+0.5Y−100i gives L=65 at Y=100 and i=.05.

check.prompt: At fixed r, why can higher expected inflation reduce money demand?
check.answer: It raises i≈r+πᵉ and the opportunity cost of holding zero-interest money.

concepts.title: Exact Fisher arithmetic
concepts.explain: Nominal returns measure money growth, while real returns measure purchasing-power growth. Divide the gross nominal payoff by gross inflation to find the real payoff.
steps: Convert percentages into decimals.
Divide gross returns.
Use subtraction only as a small-rate approximation.
concepts.increase: At fixed i, higher realized inflation lowers the realized real return.
concepts.decrease: At fixed i, lower realized inflation raises the realized real return.
concepts.edge: The approximation is least accurate for large inflation or rates. It also distinguishes realized from expected real returns.

check.prompt: If nominal interest is zero and prices fall 2%, is the real return zero?

concepts.title: The Fisher effect holds other causes fixed
concepts.explain: For a fixed expected real rate, higher expected inflation raises the nominal rate. The lecture uses the approximate one-for-one relation. In observed data, the real rate can also change.
concepts.formula: i≈r+πᵉ; exact gross relation gives i=r+πᵉ+rπᵉ
steps: Separate expected inflation from realized inflation.
Hold r fixed for the Fisher-effect comparison.
State whether the calculation is approximate or exact.
concepts.increase: A 2 percentage point rise in πᵉ raises i by approximately 2 points when r is fixed.
concepts.decrease: A 2 point fall lowers i by approximately 2 points under the same condition.
concepts.edge: A positive nominal rate can coexist with a negative expected real rate. Rational expectations also need not equal every realized outcome.
concepts.example: r≈3%,πᵉ≈4% implies i≈7%. If πᵉ becomes 1%, i≈4%.

check.prompt: Does an observed higher nominal rate always mean tighter real borrowing conditions?
check.answer: No. It can reflect higher expected inflation rather than higher r.

concepts.title: One asset-market condition can be enough
concepts.explain: With wealth held in only money and nonmonetary assets, consistent portfolio budgets link excess demands. If money demand equals supply, nonmonetary asset demand must also equal its supply.
concepts.formula: M/P=L(Y,i) represents asset-market equilibrium in the two-asset setup
steps: Sum the feasible asset demands.
Use the wealth identity.
Infer the residual market balance from money-market clearing.
concepts.increase: Excess money demand implies an offsetting excess supply of nonmonetary assets in this setup.
concepts.decrease: Excess money supply implies an offsetting excess demand for nonmonetary assets.
concepts.edge: Walras’ law needs consistent budgets and the full relevant set of markets. It does not mean every market clears at arbitrary prices.
concepts.example: If total wealth is 100, supplied money 40 and bonds 60, desired money 50 implies desired bonds 50.

check.prompt: If the money market clears, can the bond market have independent excess demand in this two-asset system?
