check.answer: No, not when the portfolio budget identity holds.

concepts.title: Bond trades transmit money-market pressure
concepts.explain: With Y, P and expected inflation fixed, an excess money supply makes people seek bonds. Bond prices rise and yields fall until desired real money holdings absorb the supply.
concepts.formula: Fixed-payoff bond yield = payoff/bond price −1
steps: Compare M/P with desired L.
Identify which asset people try to buy.
Follow bond prices and yields to the new equilibrium.
concepts.increase: More M at fixed P creates excess real balances, raising bond demand and lowering r in the baseline short-run comparison.
concepts.decrease: Less M creates excess money demand, causing bond sales and higher r.
concepts.edge: People exchanging money for bonds do not destroy aggregate M. The equilibrium changes because the yield changes desired holdings.
concepts.example: A one-period bond paying 110 yields 10% at price 100, but only 4.7619% at price 105.

check.prompt: Why do bond prices and yields move in opposite directions?
check.answer: The fixed future payoff is divided by a changing purchase price.

concepts.title: Long-run money equilibrium determines P
concepts.explain: In the classical long run, the labor market determines Y*, the goods market determines r, and the asset market determines P. Holding Y, r and expected inflation fixed makes P proportional to M.
concepts.formula: P=M/L(Y,r+πᵉ)
steps: Solve the real side first.
Evaluate the real money demand.
Choose the price level that makes real supply equal demand.
concepts.increase: A 20% increase in M raises P20% if real money demand is unchanged.
concepts.decrease: A 20% reduction in M lowers P20% under the same conditions.
concepts.edge: If the money change alters expected inflation or real money demand, simple proportionality needs rechecking. A one-time level change is not permanently higher inflation.
concepts.example: M=300 and L=150 imply P=2. M=450 with the same L implies P=3.

check.prompt: Does doubling M necessarily double real balances in this long-run case?
check.answer: No. P doubles, so M/P remains equal to unchanged L.

concepts.title: Exact growth and small-change approximations
concepts.explain: Growth of a product is approximately the sum of component growth rates. Growth of a ratio is approximately their difference. Finite changes require the gross-growth formula.
concepts.formula: For z=xy,1+g_z=(1+g_x)(1+g_y); for z=x/y,1+g_z=(1+g_x)/(1+g_y)
steps: Write the gross-growth factors.
Multiply or divide them.
Subtract 1 and compare with the linear approximation.
concepts.increase: If both x and y increase, their product increases by more than the sum of their simple growth rates because of the positive cross term.
concepts.decrease: If both decline, the product decline is smaller in magnitude than the sum of the separate declines.
concepts.edge: A rate rising from 4% to 5% increases by 1 percentage point and 25%, not 1%. Growth from a zero baseline is undefined.
concepts.example: A 10% rise in M and 5% rise in L give exact inflation 1.10/1.05−1=4.7619%, approximately 5%.

check.prompt: Can a 10% rise followed by a 10% fall restore the starting level?
check.answer: No. 1.10×0.90=0.99, so the final level is 1% lower.

concepts.title: Elasticities convert causes into demand growth
concepts.explain: An elasticity is a proportional response, not the coefficient of a linear demand function. The growth approximation weights each argument’s growth by its elasticity.
concepts.formula: ηLY=L_Y·Y/L; ηLi=L_i·i/L; π≈gM−ηLYgY−ηLig_i
steps: Differentiate L with respect to the argument.
Multiply by argument/L to obtain elasticity.
Apply percentage changes, not percentage-point changes, inside the growth formula.
concepts.increase: Higher Y raises L according to ηLY and reduces inflation for a given money-growth rate. Higher i lowers L when ηLi<0, increasing the implied P growth.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y reduces L and raises implied inflation at fixed money growth. Lower i raises L and reduces implied inflation.
concepts.edge: Linear-function elasticities vary with Y,i and L. At i=0, percentage growth of i is undefined even though a level derivative still exists.

check.prompt: Is the coefficient−100 an interest elasticity?
check.answer: No. It is a level derivative. Multiply it by i/L to obtain elasticity.

concepts.title: Monetary financing and the fiscal constraint
concepts.explain: The lecture defines hyperinflation as inflation of at least 50% per month. Rapid money creation can finance spending when other financing is unavailable. Stopping it sustainably may require spending cuts or tax reform.
concepts.formula: π≈gM−gL; fiscal financing pressure can drive gM
steps: Trace the government financing need.
Connect money creation to nominal demand and prices.
Check whether the fiscal gap remains after monetary restraint.
concepts.increase: Faster money growth tends to raise inflation when real money-demand growth does not offset it.
concepts.decrease: Slower money growth reduces inflation pressure, but sustainable stabilization may require replacing the lost financing.
concepts.edge: Lower inflation is disinflation and can leave P rising. Deflation means P falls. Money-demand collapse can amplify inflation.
concepts.example: Prices rising 50% per month for 12 months multiply by 1.5¹²≈129.75.

check.prompt: Is stopping money printing costless if the government still has an unfunded deficit?
check.answer: No. Another financing source or a fiscal adjustment is needed.

concepts.title: Match the policy instrument to the institution
concepts.explain: The lecture uses an exogenous-M model to study mechanisms. It also distinguishes the Fed’s interest-rate-centered practice from MAS’s exchange-rate-centered framework. These institutional notes do not turn this course into an open-economy model.
concepts.formula: A model’s policy variable is an assumption, not a complete institutional description
steps: Identify which institution is being discussed.
Identify its policy instrument in the lecture.
Keep the abstract comparative-static model distinct from practice.
concepts.increase: In the model, increasing M shifts real money supply at fixed P. In institutional analysis, the operating target can differ.
concepts.decrease: Reducing M reverses that model comparison, while practical policy transmission depends on the operating framework.
concepts.edge: Do not infer that MAS simply targets the same domestic policy rate as the Fed. The lecture stresses Singapore’s import exposure and exchange-rate influence on prices.
concepts.example: A textbook problem specifying M exogenously should be solved with that assumption even if the institution uses an interest-rate target in practice.

check.prompt: Why might the exchange rate matter strongly for Singapore inflation?
check.answer: Imports have a large role in expenditure, so exchange rates affect domestic-currency import prices.

concepts.title: Expected future money can affect today
concepts.explain: Anticipating a future cigarette shipment can raise expected inflation before the shipment arrives. At a given real rate, the higher nominal opportunity cost reduces demand for cigarette balances, raising today’s price level if M is unchanged.
concepts.formula: πᵉ↑ → i↑ → L↓ → P=M/L↑, holding r,Y,M fixed
steps: Separate the announcement date from the shipment date.
Update expected inflation and money demand.
Solve the current price level using current money supply.
concepts.increase: A more credible larger future shipment can increase expected depreciation of cigarette money and raise current prices through lower L.
concepts.decrease: Cancellation of an expected shipment can reduce expected inflation, increase L and lower current prices under the same assumptions.
concepts.edge: The outcome requires an expectations response. An unanticipated shipment cannot change behavior before anyone knows about it.
concepts.example: With current M=200, a fall in desired real balances from 100 to 80 raises P from 2 to 2.5 before M changes.

check.prompt: Must the current nominal money stock rise for current prices to rise?
check.answer: No. A fall in real money demand can raise P at unchanged M.

lessons.title: Reading business cycles
lessons.subtitle: Classify direction and timing without confusing either with causation.

concepts.title: Peaks, troughs and phases
concepts.explain: A peak marks the change from expansion to contraction. A trough marks the change from contraction to expansion. A complete cycle can be measured from peak to peak or trough to trough.
concepts.formula: Expansion = rising activity; contraction = declining activity
steps: Observe the direction of activity over time.
Locate reversals.
Label the intervals between turning points.
concepts.increase: Rising activity after a trough is expansion even if the level remains low.
concepts.decrease: Falling activity after a peak is contraction even if the level remains high.
concepts.edge: A single noisy observation may not establish a turning point. Revisions and persistence matter.
concepts.example: Output 100,104,108,105,101,103 has a local peak at 108 and trough at 101.

check.prompt: Is the trough itself the entire recession?
check.answer: No. It is a turning point at the end of the contraction.

concepts.title: Growth and position relative to trend are different
concepts.explain: An economy can grow while remaining below trend, or shrink while remaining above trend. The lecture compares textbook definitions based on changes in activity with definitions based on deviations from trend.
concepts.formula: Gap=(Y−trend)/trend; growth=(Yₜ−Yₜ₋₁)/Yₜ₋₁
steps: Compute growth from successive output observations.
Compute the gap using the relevant trend.
State the definition before labeling boom or recession.
concepts.increase: Output can increase from 90 to 94 while trend rises from 100 to 102, giving expansion but still a negative gap.
concepts.decrease: Output can decrease from 110 to 108 while trend is 100, giving contraction with a positive gap.
concepts.edge: Different textbooks need not use boom and recession identically. Do not silently swap definitions halfway through an argument.
concepts.example: Y=102 with trend 100 gives a 2% positive gap regardless of whether Y was rising or falling.

check.prompt: Does a negative output gap necessarily imply negative current growth?
check.answer: No. Level relative to trend and change over time are different measurements.

concepts.title: Recurrent does not mean clockwork
concepts.explain: Expansions and contractions recur, but their durations and sizes are irregular. Persistence means recent increases or decreases tend to be followed by further movement in the same direction.
concepts.formula: Recurrent ≠ periodic; persistent ≠ permanent
steps: Distinguish repeating patterns from fixed intervals.
Inspect how changes continue across periods.
Recognize that persistence does not identify the next turning point exactly.
concepts.increase: Several consecutive increases can indicate persistence without establishing a fixed expansion duration.
concepts.decrease: Several decreases can indicate persistence without implying activity falls forever.
concepts.edge: A forecast based on a fixed five-year cycle is not justified by recurrence alone.
concepts.example: Cycles lasting 4,7 and 3 years recur but are not periodic.

check.prompt: Can a persistent series still turn at a trough?
check.answer: Yes. Persistence is a tendency, not a prohibition on reversals.

concepts.title: Direction compares comovement
concepts.explain: Procyclical variables move with aggregate activity, countercyclical variables move against it, and acyclical variables show no clear systematic pattern. Classification concerns a pattern across observations.
concepts.formula: Procyclical positive comovement; countercyclical negative comovement
steps: Compare the variable with aggregate activity.
Use both expansion and contraction observations.
Avoid inferring a stable pattern from one episode.
concepts.increase: A procyclical variable tends to rise in expansion. A countercyclical variable tends to fall.
concepts.decrease: A procyclical variable tends to fall in contraction. A countercyclical variable tends to rise.
concepts.edge: Acyclical does not mean constant. It can fluctuate strongly without systematic cycle-related comovement.
concepts.example: If output rises while a variable regularly falls, and output falls while it rises, the variable is countercyclical.

check.prompt: Does a strongly varying series have to be procyclical?
check.answer: No. Volatility and cyclicality are separate properties.

concepts.title: Timing compares turning points
concepts.explain: Leading variables turn before aggregate activity, lagging variables after it, and coincident variables at approximately the same time. Timing and direction are independent classifications.
concepts.formula: A variable can be countercyclical and leading at the same time
steps: Align dates for the variable and output.
Locate corresponding turning points.
Report timing separately from direction.
concepts.increase: A variable beginning to rise before output rises may lead, but whether it is procyclical depends on the direction pattern.
concepts.decrease: A countercyclical leading variable may begin to rise before output begins to fall.
concepts.edge: Leading association does not prove causation or ensure perfect forecasting. False signals can occur.
concepts.example: A countercyclical indicator peaks in March before output reaches a trough in May. It leads by two months.

check.prompt: Can a lagging variable move in the same direction as output?
check.answer: Yes. It is then procyclical and lagging.

concepts.title: Facts constrain theories without proving them
concepts.explain: A useful business-cycle explanation should account for several observed comovements. The lecture asks students to know the definitions rather than memorize every variable classification. Correlation is evidence to explain, not causal identification.
concepts.formula: Shared movement can arise from causation, reverse causation or common shocks
steps: State the observed pattern.
List mechanisms compatible with it.
Ask what additional evidence separates those mechanisms.
concepts.increase: Stronger comovement may make a pattern more informative but does not by itself identify a causal channel.
concepts.decrease: Weaker or unstable comovement can challenge a theory that predicts a tight relation.
concepts.edge: A leading money series need not prove money shocks cause every cycle. Policy may respond to information about future activity.
concepts.example: Money growth can lead output because policy causes output changes or because policy responds to an anticipated downturn.

check.prompt: Why are revised data relevant to cycle dating?
check.answer: Initial releases can misidentify a temporary fluctuation as a lasting turning point.

concepts.title: Cycles can be shared across economies
concepts.explain: Countries often exhibit related cycle movements. Common shocks and cross-border transmission are possible explanations, but synchronized outcomes alone do not identify which channel caused them.
concepts.formula: Comovement across countries is an empirical pattern, not a unique structural equation
steps: Compare direction and turning dates across countries.
Identify potential shared or transmitted shocks.
Distinguish correlation from a causal claim.
concepts.increase: An expansion in several countries at once is international comovement.
concepts.decrease: A contraction in several countries at once is also international comovement.
concepts.edge: Similar patterns do not mean every country peaks on the same date or experiences the same amplitude.
concepts.example: If countries A and B both contract after a global oil disruption, a common shock is plausible but must be tested against alternatives.

check.prompt: Does synchronized recession prove one country caused the other’s recession?
check.answer: No. Both may be responding to a common disturbance.

lessons.title: IS, LM, FE and aggregate demand
lessons.subtitle: Trace every curve back to the market it clears.

concepts.title: Three markets, three conditions
concepts.explain: Competitive households and firms take prices as given. General equilibrium requires labor, goods and assets to clear simultaneously. An IS–LM intersection clears only goods and assets until it also lies on FE.
concepts.formula: Nˢ = Nᵈ; Sᵈ = Iᵈ; M/P = L(Y,r+πᵉ)
steps: Solve labor for N* and Y*.
Use goods equilibrium to determine r at Y*.
Use money equilibrium to determine P.
concepts.increase: If demand pushes the IS–LM intersection above FE, goods and assets clear at excessive demand for full-employment output. Prices subsequently rise in the adjustment model.
concepts.decrease: If the intersection is below FE, deficient demand depresses output in the sticky-price short run. Falling prices raise real balances and help restore output.
concepts.edge: An economy may have unemployment at full employment because frictional and structural unemployment remain. General equilibrium does not mean u = 0.
concepts.example: Given FE at Y = 100, IS at r = 10 − 0.05Y implies r = 5. If L = 2Y − 10r = 150 and M = 300, equilibrium P = 2.

check.prompt: Does an IS–LM intersection always clear the labor market?
check.answer: No. It must also be on the FE line for all three markets to clear.

concepts.title: The FE line
concepts.explain: FE records combinations of output and real interest consistent with labor-market equilibrium. In the course model, r does not enter that labor equilibrium, so FE is vertical.
concepts.formula: Y = Y* = AF(K,N*)
steps: Find the labor-market equilibrium.
Insert N* into production.
Draw a vertical line at the resulting Y*.
concepts.increase: Higher productivity, capital or labor supply can raise Y* and shift FE right, with the labor-market response included.
concepts.decrease: Lower productivity, capital or labor supply can lower Y* and shift FE left.
concepts.edge: A change in r is not itself an FE shifter in this model. In the efficiency-wage Keynesian model, a labor-supply shift need not change Y*.
concepts.example: If Y* changes from 100 to 110, FE moves right by 10 at every r. The line does not rotate.

check.prompt: Why is FE vertical rather than upward sloping?
check.answer: The model pins down potential output in the labor market independently of the real interest rate.

concepts.title: Deriving IS from saving and investment
concepts.explain: Hold output fixed and find the interest rate equating desired saving and desired investment. Repeat at other output levels. Higher output raises saving when the MPC is below one, so a lower rate is needed to restore equality.
concepts.formula: Sᵈ = Y − Cᵈ − G = Iᵈ
steps: Raise Y in the loanable-funds diagram.
Saving shifts right because consumption rises less than income.
The clearing r falls, giving another point on IS.
concepts.increase: Higher Y moves down along an unchanged IS curve, provided other determinants stay fixed.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y shifts saving left in the underlying loanable-funds diagram, raises the clearing r and moves up along IS.
concepts.edge: One saving–investment intersection is one point on IS. It is not a whole IS curve.

check.prompt: Why does saving shift while IS itself does not when deriving IS?
check.answer: Y varies to trace the locus. Exogenous spending determinants remain fixed.

concepts.title: IS algebra and tax rules
concepts.explain: Substitute consumption, investment and the stated tax rule into goods equilibrium. Keep income-induced taxes separate from lump-sum taxes. The slope reflects spending leakage and interest sensitivity.
concepts.formula: C = c₀ + c(Y−T) − ar; I = i₀ − br; T = T₀+tY; [1−c(1−t)]Y = c₀−cT₀+i₀+G−(a+b)r
steps: Substitute the tax rule into C.
Collect all terms involving Y on the left.
Solve for r or Y, keeping units consistent.
concepts.increase: A higher marginal tax rate t increases spending leakage and makes IS steeper in an r-versus-Y graph, holding a+b fixed.
concepts.decrease: A lower t reduces leakage and flattens IS when 0<c<1.
concepts.edge: If a+b = 0, the usual solved expression for r divides by zero. Goods equilibrium then pins Y independently of r.
concepts.example: For c = 0.8 and t = 0.25, the output coefficient is 1−0.8×0.75 = 0.4, not 0.2.

check.prompt: With c = 0.75 and t = 0.2, what is 1−c(1−t)?

concepts.title: What shifts IS
concepts.explain: An exogenous rise in desired spending at a given Y and r creates excess goods demand. A higher r is required to reduce spending and restore equilibrium at that Y. IS shifts up and right.
concepts.formula: At fixed Y, ΔIᵈ > ΔSᵈ implies a higher clearing r
steps: Identify the direct change at fixed Y and r.
Translate it into saving or investment.
Determine the interest change that restores equality.
concepts.increase: Higher autonomous consumption, wealth, expected future income, future MPK or G can shift IS right. A tax cut does so when Ricardian equivalence fails.
concepts.decrease: Lower autonomous consumption, wealth, expected future income, future MPK or G can shift IS left. A tax rise does so when it reduces desired consumption.
concepts.edge: A tax-timing change with fixed government spending leaves IS unchanged under Ricardian equivalence. Do not treat every tax cut as stimulus.
concepts.example: With r = 12 − 0.1Y, a rise of 2 in the intercept gives r = 14 − 0.1Y. At r = 4, desired equilibrium Y rises from 80 to 100.

check.prompt: Does a lower r shift IS right?
check.answer: No. It causes movement along IS unless an exogenous determinant also changes.

concepts.title: Bonds transmit money-market adjustment
concepts.explain: When people collectively want less money than supplied, they try to buy nonmonetary assets. Bond prices rise and yields fall, making money relatively more attractive until people willingly hold the existing supply.
concepts.formula: Bond price = fixed future payoff / (1+i)
steps: Compare money supplied with money demanded.
Infer whether people buy or sell bonds.
Use the inverse relation between bond price and yield.
concepts.increase: Excess money supply induces bond purchases, higher bond prices and lower nominal yields. With expected inflation fixed, r falls too.
concepts.decrease: Excess money demand induces bond sales, lower bond prices and higher yields. With expected inflation fixed, r rises too.
concepts.edge: One person can reduce cash holdings by buying a bond, but the buyer transfers money to someone else. Aggregate money does not vanish.
concepts.example: A bond paying 110 next year costs 100 at i = 10%. If its price rises to 104.76, its yield is approximately 5%.

check.prompt: If everyone wants to obtain more money by selling bonds, what happens to bond yields?
check.answer: Bond prices fall and yields rise until money demand is brought into line with supply.

concepts.title: Deriving LM from the money market
concepts.explain: At a given price level and nominal money supply, real balances are fixed. Higher output raises transactions demand, so interest must rise to discourage money holding and clear the asset market.
concepts.formula: M/P = L(Y,r+πᵉ)
steps: Hold M, P and expected inflation fixed.
Raise Y and shift real money demand right.
Find the higher clearing r and plot the new point on LM.
concepts.increase: Higher Y moves up along a given LM curve because transactions demand rises.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y reduces transactions demand, allowing a lower r and a move down along LM.
concepts.edge: A change in Y shifts the money-demand curve in its own diagram but traces movement along LM.
concepts.example: For L = 2Y − 10r and M/P = 100, LM is r = 0.2Y − 10. Raising Y from 80 to 90 raises r from 6 to 8.

check.prompt: What is held fixed when deriving an LM curve?
check.answer: Nominal money supply, price level, expected inflation and other money-demand determinants.

concepts.title: LM algebra and expected inflation
concepts.explain: Money demand depends on nominal interest because that is the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing money. In an r-versus-Y diagram, substitute i ≈ r + πᵉ before solving.
concepts.formula: L = l₀ + kY − h(r+πᵉ); r = (l₀−M/P)/h + (k/h)Y − πᵉ
steps: Write real money supply equal to real demand.
Substitute nominal interest with real interest plus expected inflation.
Collect r to reveal the slope and intercept.
concepts.increase: Higher expected inflation shifts LM down in real-interest space. At a fixed r it raises i and lowers money demand.
concepts.decrease: Lower expected inflation shifts LM up. At a fixed r it lowers i and raises money demand.
concepts.edge: With the nominal-rate bound binding, the standard unconstrained linear LM is not valid below i = 0.
concepts.example: If M/P = 100, l₀ = 20, k = 2, h = 10 and πᵉ = 1 in consistent rate units, LM is r = 0.2Y − 9.

check.prompt: Does expected inflation mechanically change current M/P?
check.answer: No. It changes money demand through nominal interest, unless current P or M also changes.

concepts.title: Real balances and LM shifts
concepts.explain: LM shifts when real money supply changes relative to money demand at a given output. More real balances require a lower rate to make people hold them.
concepts.formula: Real balances = M/P
steps: Compute whether M/P rises or falls.
At fixed Y, compare money supply with demand.
Adjust r to clear the market.
concepts.increase: An increase in M or a decrease in P raises real balances and shifts LM down and right.
concepts.decrease: A decrease in M or an increase in P lowers real balances and shifts LM up and left.
concepts.edge: If M and P change proportionately, real balances and LM are unchanged, all else equal.
concepts.example: M rises from 200 to 220 while P rises from 2 to 2.2. M/P remains 100, so there is no net LM shift.

check.prompt: A rise in autonomous money demand with M/P fixed shifts LM in which direction?
check.answer: Up and left because a higher r is needed to reduce money demand at any Y.

concepts.title: Solving short-run and long-run equilibria
concepts.explain: At fixed prices, solve IS and LM for Y and r. In full equilibrium, impose FE first, use IS for r and solve money equilibrium for P. The unknown price level makes the distinction essential.
concepts.formula: IS r = a−bY; LM r = c+dY; YSR = (a−c)/(b+d)
steps: For the short run, use the given P in LM.
Equate IS and LM to solve Y and r.
For the long run, replace Y with Y* and solve P.
concepts.increase: A higher IS intercept raises short-run Y and r. With fixed Y*, long-run r rises and P adjusts.
concepts.decrease: A lower IS intercept reduces short-run Y and r. With fixed Y*, long-run r falls and P adjusts.
concepts.edge: A calculated nonpositive money demand cannot support a positive price level with positive M. Check the domain before treating an algebraic solution as economic equilibrium.
concepts.example: IS r = 20−0.1Y and LM r = −4+0.2Y give Y = 80, r = 12. If Y* = 90, this is a short-run output gap of −10.

check.prompt: Must the short-run intersection equal Y*?
check.answer: No. Price rigidity can keep the economy away from full employment.

concepts.title: Deriving aggregate demand
concepts.explain: AD is the set of IS–LM output equilibria generated by different price levels. A higher P reduces real balances, raises r and crowds out interest-sensitive spending.
concepts.formula: P↑ → M/P↓ → LM up → r↑ → Cᵈ and Iᵈ↓ → Y↓
steps: Choose a price level and solve IS–LM.
Change only P and solve again.
Plot the resulting pairs of P and Y.
concepts.increase: An increase in P moves upward and left along a fixed AD curve. It shifts LM, not AD itself.
concepts.decrease: A decrease in P moves downward and right along AD because real balances rise and spending recovers.
concepts.edge: AD is not an ordinary consumer demand curve. Its downward slope comes from aggregate market equilibrium.
concepts.example: For IS r = 10−0.1Y and L = 2Y−10r, M/P = 3Y−100. Thus Y = (100+M/P)/3.

check.prompt: Does a price increase shift AD left?
check.answer: No. With other determinants fixed it generates movement along AD.

concepts.title: AD shifts from either market
concepts.explain: An exogenous change that raises IS–LM equilibrium output at every fixed P shifts AD right. Both goods-market and money-market changes can do this.
concepts.formula: AD shift = change in equilibrium Y at a fixed P
steps: Freeze the price level.
Work out the IS or LM shift.
Read the change in intersection output.
concepts.increase: Higher M, G, autonomous consumption or expected inflation can raise output at each P and shift AD right in the standard model.
concepts.decrease: Lower M, G, autonomous consumption or expected inflation can reduce output at each P and shift AD left.
concepts.edge: A pure change in Y* shifts LRAS and FE, not AD, if spending and money-demand parameters remain unchanged.
concepts.example: An unexpected money contraction reduces M/P at every P, shifts LM up and yields a leftward AD shift.

check.prompt: If higher expected inflation shifts LM down, what happens to AD under the standard fixed-P setup?
check.answer: It shifts right as lower r raises desired spending and output.

concepts.title: Two supply curves, two horizons
concepts.explain: Lecture 6 assumes prices fixed in the short run, so firms meet demand at the preset price and SRAS is horizontal. With full price adjustment, output returns to the supply-determined Y*, giving vertical LRAS.
concepts.formula: SRAS P = preset P; LRAS Y = Y*
steps: Identify whether prices can adjust.
Use AD with the appropriate supply curve.
Track the output gap and subsequent price adjustment.
concepts.increase: An AD increase raises Y at a fixed P initially. With fixed Y*, prices later rise until Y returns to Y*.
concepts.decrease: An AD decrease lowers Y at a fixed P initially. Prices later fall until real balances support Y*.
concepts.edge: The horizontal SRAS here differs from the upward-sloping misperceptions SRAS. Select a model before interpreting its slope.
concepts.example: AD rises while Y* stays 100 and P is initially 2. Short-run Y can be 110. Long-run Y is 100 at a higher P.

check.prompt: Does vertical LRAS mean output can never change?
check.answer: No. Supply-side changes shift LRAS by changing Y*.

concepts.title: Monetary expansion and contraction
concepts.explain: With initially sticky prices, changing nominal money changes real balances, interest and demand. Once prices fully adjust and real determinants stay fixed, real balances and real outcomes return to their initial levels.
concepts.formula: Long-run ΔP/P = ΔM/M when Y*, r and money-demand determinants stay fixed
steps: Shift LM immediately at the original P.
Read short-run r and Y.
Let P adjust until the intersection returns to FE.
concepts.increase: More M lowers r and raises Y and interest-sensitive spending initially. Later P rises, LM shifts back and real outcomes return.
concepts.decrease: Less M raises r and lowers Y and interest-sensitive spending initially. Later P falls, LM shifts back and real outcomes return.
concepts.edge: Neutrality is a model result with unchanged real determinants. It is not a claim that money is neutral during every transition.
concepts.example: A permanent 20% rise in M ultimately raises P by 20% in this setup. A 20% fall in M ultimately lowers P by 20%, rather than undoing a prior 20% rise.

check.prompt: After a long-run monetary expansion, must nominal wages remain unchanged?
check.answer: No. With unchanged real wages and a higher P, nominal wages rise proportionately.

concepts.title: Fiscal policy with fixed FE
concepts.explain: A spending expansion shifts IS right. At fixed P the interest rise partly crowds out private spending. With fixed potential output, further price adjustment eventually makes total private spending fall by the government-spending increase.
concepts.formula: At fixed Y*, ΔC + ΔI = −ΔG
steps: Increase G and shift IS.
Solve the short-run intersection.
Raise P and shift LM until Y returns to fixed Y*.
concepts.increase: Higher G raises short-run Y and r. In the fixed-FE long run, P and r rise while C+I falls by ΔG.
concepts.decrease: Lower G reduces short-run Y and r. In the fixed-FE long run, P and r fall while private spending expands by the released resources.
concepts.edge: Full crowding out concerns C+I together. Investment alone need not fall by ΔG. The Classical wealth effect may also shift FE.
concepts.example: If G rises 12 and long-run C falls 5 at unchanged Y, I must fall 7.

check.prompt: Why is it incorrect to claim I always falls one-for-one with G?
check.answer: Consumption can also change, so the resource identity constrains total private spending.

concepts.title: Money-demand sensitivity and policy
concepts.explain: The slope of LM is the income sensitivity of money demand divided by its interest sensitivity. A flat LM allows fiscal demand changes with little rate crowding out. A money-supply change has a smaller interest effect when money demand is very interest-sensitive.
concepts.formula: LM slope = k/h; for Y = A−Br and M/P = kY−hr, ∂Y/∂A = h/(h+kB), ∂Y/∂(M/P) = B/(h+kB)
steps: Hold the other behavioral coefficients fixed.
Change h and observe the LM slope.
Compare the resulting output response to the same policy change.
concepts.increase: Higher h flattens LM, strengthens fiscal effects and weakens the output effect of a fixed increase in real balances.
concepts.decrease: Lower h steepens LM, weakens fiscal effects and strengthens the output effect of a fixed increase in real balances.
concepts.edge: A flatter curve from changing k rather than h is a different experiment. The comparative claim requires stating what changes.
concepts.example: With k = 1 and B = 2, raising h from 2 to 6 raises ∂Y/∂A from 1/2 to 3/4 and lowers ∂Y/∂(M/P) from 1/2 to 1/4.

check.prompt: Why is fiscal policy stronger with more interest-sensitive money demand?
check.answer: A smaller rise in r is sufficient to absorb the extra transactions demand, so less private spending is crowded out.

concepts.title: The vertical LM limit
concepts.explain: If money demand depends only on income, money-market equilibrium pins output independently of r. LM is vertical. A fiscal shift changes r at that fixed output, while a change in real balances shifts the output level itself.
concepts.formula: L = kY; Y = M/(Pk)
steps: Set the interest coefficient to zero in money demand.
Solve directly for Y, without dividing by that coefficient.
Intersect the resulting vertical LM with IS.
concepts.increase: Higher G raises r but leaves Y unchanged at fixed P and M. Higher M raises the output level allowed by the money market.
concepts.decrease: Lower G reduces r without changing Y. Lower M reduces the output consistent with money-market clearing.
concepts.edge: Vertical LM does not imply vertical IS or that money is ineffective. It is the opposite monetary-policy limit from the liquidity trap.
concepts.example: If k = 2 and M/P = 200, Y = 100. An IS shift from r = 20−0.1Y to r = 24−0.1Y raises r from 10 to 14.

check.prompt: Can fiscal expansion raise Y with vertical LM and fixed real balances?
check.answer: No. It raises the clearing interest rate and crowds out the added spending.

concepts.title: The nominal-rate bound and liquidity trap
concepts.explain: At zero nominal interest, money and short bonds have the same financial return in the simplified model. Additional money can be willingly held without a further interest fall. The relevant lower bound is on i, not r.
concepts.formula: i ≈ r + πᵉ; i ≥ 0 implies r ≥ −πᵉ
steps: Use the Fisher relation to find the real-rate floor.
Identify whether the flat segment is binding.
Separate cash injections from policies that move spending or expected inflation.
concepts.increase: While trapped, more M alone need not raise Y. Higher G can raise Y without interest crowding out until the flat segment ends. Higher expected inflation lowers the real-rate floor.
concepts.decrease: A G reduction lowers Y along the flat segment. Lower expected inflation raises the real-rate floor and can deepen weak demand. A money contraction has no effect only while balances remain sufficient to stay in the trap.
concepts.edge: The course uses a zero nominal bound as an approximation. Small negative nominal rates are possible in practice. A real rate below zero is fully compatible with i = 0 and positive expected inflation.
concepts.example: At i = 0 and expected inflation 3%, approximate r = −3%. With expected deflation of 3%, r = +3%, which can restrain spending.

check.prompt: At zero nominal interest, does expected deflation make borrowing cheaper in real terms?
check.answer: No. It raises the real interest rate because r ≈ i − πᵉ.

lessons.title: New Classical and RBC models
lessons.subtitle: Separate flexible prices, real shocks and imperfect information.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 7- The New Classical and RBC Models.pdf

concepts.title: Real shocks and business cycles
concepts.explain: RBC attributes major fluctuations to real disturbances, especially productivity, with flexible wages and prices keeping markets clear. Changes in output can be changes in potential output rather than demand gaps.
concepts.formula: Y* = AF(K,N*); MPN = w
steps: Identify the real shock.
Solve the labor-market and production response.
Use IS and money equilibrium for r and P.
concepts.increase: A beneficial temporary productivity shock raises labor demand, real wages, employment and Y* under the standard upward-sloping labor supply.
concepts.decrease: An adverse temporary shock lowers labor demand, real wages, employment and Y*.
concepts.edge: RBC does not require productivity to literally be new technology. Energy availability, management and input quality can affect productive efficiency.
concepts.example: A temporary energy disruption lowers effective productivity. A lower Y is consistent with market clearing rather than proof of deficient AD.

check.prompt: Does a fall in actual output necessarily mean Y is below Y* in RBC?
check.answer: No. Potential output itself may fall with the real shock.

concepts.title: Following productivity through all markets
concepts.explain: In the lecture experiment, a temporary productivity shock shifts FE while IS is unchanged. The full-employment output change alters saving, which changes r. Money demand then determines P.
concepts.formula: Negative A → FE left → lower Y on IS → higher r → lower L → higher P
steps: Shift labor demand and solve Y*.
Move to the new Y* along unchanged IS.
Use the induced Y and r to determine real money demand and P.
concepts.increase: Higher temporary A raises Y*, lowers r along IS and raises money demand through both Y and r, so P falls with M fixed.
concepts.decrease: Lower temporary A reduces Y*, raises r and lowers money demand through both channels, so P rises.
concepts.edge: If the shock changes expected future productivity or income, IS may also shift. The simple chain assumes those additional effects away.
concepts.example: With IS r = 15−0.1Y, Y* falling from 100 to 90 raises r from 5 to 6. L = 2Y−10r falls from 150 to 120, so fixed M = 300 raises P from 2 to 2.5.

check.prompt: Why does an adverse temporary productivity shock raise P in this lecture case?
check.answer: Both lower Y and higher r reduce real money demand. Fixed nominal M then requires a higher P.

concepts.title: Fiscal policy can shift FE
concepts.explain: Higher government purchases require current or future taxes. With leisure normal, households feel poorer and supply more labor. Thus Classical fiscal policy can affect output even with flexible prices.
concepts.formula: G↑ → lifetime private resources↓ → leisure↓ → Nˢ↑ → N*↑ → Y*↑
steps: Trace the tax-financing wealth effect.
Shift labor supply and FE.
Also shift IS and solve the new full equilibrium.
concepts.increase: Higher temporary G raises labor supply and potential output. IS shifts right as national saving falls. In the lecture configuration r and P rise too.
concepts.decrease: Lower G reduces the tax burden, increases desired leisure and shifts labor supply and FE left. IS shifts left as saving rises.
concepts.edge: The sign of the net price change depends on the relative shifts. The lecture assumes the new IS with original LM intersects to the right of the new FE.
concepts.example: Suppose G rises 10 and Y rises 4. The resource identity implies C+I falls 6, not 10.

check.prompt: Why is fixed-output fiscal crowding out not universal across the course?
check.answer: The Classical labor-supply wealth effect can raise Y*, whereas the stated Keynesian fiscal case holds FE fixed.

concepts.title: Flexible prices and monetary neutrality
concepts.explain: With fully flexible prices and no information friction, nominal money does not change the labor and goods-market equations that determine real outcomes. P adjusts to keep desired real balances unchanged.
concepts.formula: P = M/L(Y*,r+πᵉ)
steps: Solve real variables from real markets.
Hold their determinants and expected inflation fixed.
Scale P with nominal M.
concepts.increase: A one-off rise in M raises P and nominal wages proportionately, leaving Y, N, w and r unchanged.
concepts.decrease: A one-off fall in M lowers P and nominal wages proportionately, leaving those real variables unchanged.
concepts.edge: A money-growth change can alter expected inflation and nominal interest. Do not confuse a money-level change with a permanent change in its growth rate.
concepts.example: If M and P both double, M/P and W/P are unchanged when W doubles too.

check.prompt: Does neutrality imply nominal interest must rise after every one-off increase in M?
check.answer: No. With expected inflation unchanged, i need not change.

concepts.title: Rational expectations are informed expectations
concepts.explain: Agents use available relevant information and the economic structure when forming expectations. Forecast errors remain possible because new information and genuine surprises occur.
concepts.formula: Forecast error = actual outcome − conditional expectation
steps: Specify what was known when the expectation was formed.
Identify the genuinely new information.
Separate a predictable policy rule from its surprise component.
concepts.increase: More credible information about a forthcoming expansion raises expected prices before implementation.
concepts.decrease: Credible information about a forthcoming contraction lowers expected prices.
concepts.edge: Rational expectations does not give agents tomorrow’s unknown shocks or require zero forecast error in every period.
concepts.example: A weather forecast using all available information can still be wrong because tomorrow’s realization is uncertain. That is compatible with rational expectations.

check.prompt: Can rational agents be surprised by an unforeseeable shock?
check.answer: Yes. Rational expectations rules out systematically ignoring available information, not uncertainty.

concepts.title: Own prices versus the general price level
concepts.explain: A producer sees the price of their own product more clearly than the overall price level. They want to expand when their relative price rises, but not when every price rises equally. Imperfect information can confuse the two.
concepts.formula: Relative price = own price / aggregate price level
steps: Observe the own-price change.
Form a belief about the aggregate price change.
Adjust output according to the inferred relative-price change.
concepts.increase: An unexpected aggregate price increase can be partly mistaken for a relative-price improvement, inducing additional production.
concepts.decrease: An unexpected aggregate price decrease can be partly mistaken for a relative-price deterioration, inducing less production.
concepts.edge: With complete immediate information that all prices move proportionately, there is no mistaken relative-price incentive.
concepts.example: Your selling price rises 6%. If all input and consumption prices rise 6%, your relative price is unchanged, unlike a 6% own-price rise with other prices fixed.

check.prompt: Why does an anticipated general price rise have no relative-price signal?
check.answer: Producers already expect the common price movement and do not mistake it for a change in their own relative price.

concepts.title: The surprise-output equation
concepts.explain: The misperceptions model permits output above or below potential even with flexible prices because imperfect information changes perceived relative prices. Expected price is held fixed when moving along SRAS.
concepts.formula: Y = Y* + b(P−Pᵉ), b > 0
steps: Calculate the price surprise.
Multiply it by responsiveness b.
Add the result to potential output.
concepts.increase: If P exceeds Pᵉ, output exceeds Y*.
concepts.decrease: If P falls below Pᵉ, output falls below Y*.
concepts.edge: At P = Pᵉ output equals Y*. A change in Pᵉ shifts SRAS, while a change in P moves along it.
concepts.example: For Y* = 100, b = 4 and Pᵉ = 10, P = 11 gives Y = 104 and P = 9 gives Y = 96.

check.prompt: What does larger b mean?
check.answer: A larger output response to a given unexpected price-level change, or a flatter SRAS in a P-versus-Y diagram.

concepts.title: Anticipated monetary changes
concepts.explain: If a policy is fully anticipated and credible in the misperceptions model, expected prices adjust with actual prices. AD and SRAS shift together and output stays at potential.
concepts.formula: P−Pᵉ = 0 implies Y = Y*
steps: Let agents incorporate the announced policy into Pᵉ.
Shift AD and SRAS consistently.
Check that the equilibrium price surprise is zero.
concepts.increase: A fully anticipated expansion raises P and Pᵉ together, leaving Y at Y*.
concepts.decrease: A fully anticipated contraction lowers P and Pᵉ together, leaving Y at Y*.
concepts.edge: Anticipated policy neutrality is specific to this flexible-price information model. Sticky-price Keynesian outcomes require a different analysis.
concepts.example: If both actual and expected prices rise from 100 to 110, b(P−Pᵉ) remains zero.

check.prompt: Can you assess an announcement by shifting AD while forcing Pᵉ unchanged?
check.answer: Not if the announcement is fully credible and anticipated in the model.

concepts.title: Unexpected monetary changes
concepts.explain: When money changes unexpectedly, expected prices do not fully adjust immediately. The price surprise changes output temporarily. Once information catches up, output returns to potential.
concepts.formula: Short run P ≠ Pᵉ; long run P = Pᵉ
steps: Shift AD with initial Pᵉ held fixed.
Find the short-run intersection on the original SRAS.
Update expectations and shift SRAS until Y returns to Y*.
concepts.increase: An unexpected expansion raises P and Y initially. Later Pᵉ rises, SRAS shifts up and Y returns to Y*.
concepts.decrease: An unexpected contraction lowers P and Y initially. Later Pᵉ falls, SRAS shifts down and Y returns to Y*.
concepts.edge: A predictable sequence of attempted surprises ceases to be surprising under rational expectations.
concepts.example: An unannounced monetary increase creates a positive price surprise today. Next period agents may fully anticipate the resulting price level, eliminating the output gap.

check.prompt: Why cannot the central bank permanently keep Y above Y* by repeating the same surprise?
check.answer: People learn the systematic policy pattern and incorporate it into expectations.

concepts.title: The Lucas critique and policy evaluation
concepts.explain: Historical behavioral relationships may change when the policy rule changes because agents change their expectations and decisions. A fit to past data is not automatically a reliable policy counterfactual.
concepts.formula: Policy rule change → expectations change → behavioral relationship changes
steps: Identify the historical relationship being extrapolated.
Ask whether the policy changes incentives or expectations.
Recompute behavior under the new rule.
concepts.increase: A systematic attempt to raise inflation to exploit an old Phillips tradeoff can raise expected inflation and shift that curve.
concepts.decrease: A credible disinflation rule can reduce expected inflation, altering the relationship observed under the previous regime.
concepts.edge: The critique does not say data are useless. It says policy evaluation must account for endogenous behavioral responses. RBC policy recommendations also depend on its efficiency assumptions.
concepts.example: A government cannot assume a past correlation between surprise money and output remains unchanged after it announces that money will always rise when output falls.

check.prompt: What is wrong with treating expectations as fixed after changing a predictable policy rule?
check.answer: The public can respond to the new rule, so the estimated old relationship may no longer describe behavior.

lessons.title: New Keynesian foundations
lessons.subtitle: Understand why rational firms may keep wages and prices sticky.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 8 - the New Keynesian Model.pdf

concepts.title: Demand-driven output gaps
concepts.explain: Keynesian models emphasize shifts in aggregate demand when wages and prices adjust slowly. Firms produce less and hire fewer workers because fewer goods are demanded at existing prices.
concepts.formula: Sticky P → IS–LM determines Y, which may differ from Y*
steps: Identify the demand shock.
Hold prices fixed in the immediate response.
Trace production and employment rather than assuming markets clear instantly.
concepts.increase: Higher demand raises production and employment in the short run when firms can meet it at preset prices.
concepts.decrease: Lower demand reduces production and employment, creating a negative output gap.
concepts.edge: A demand recession differs from an efficient response to a lower productive capacity in the RBC interpretation.
concepts.example: Consumer pessimism shifts IS left. At fixed P, Y falls even though machines, technology and potential output need not change.

check.prompt: Why can unemployment rise without a fall in workers’ desire to work?
check.answer: Firms require fewer workers when demand for their output falls.

concepts.title: Why wages may not clear the labor market
concepts.explain: Minimum wages, contracts, turnover costs and incentive effects can prevent the real wage from falling to the market-clearing level. A high wage can sometimes reduce a firm’s total cost by improving worker performance.
concepts.formula: Involuntary unemployment arises when Nˢ(w) > Nᵈ(w)
steps: Identify why wages resist adjustment.
Compare supply and demand at that wage.
Measure the excess labor supply.
concepts.increase: A fall in labor demand at an unchanged high wage lowers employment and increases unemployment.
concepts.decrease: A rise in labor demand at that wage increases employment and reduces excess labor supply.
concepts.edge: A wage above market clearing is not necessarily irrational for an individual firm if effort or turnover depends on pay.
concepts.example: At wage 10, 100 workers wish to work and firms hire 70. Thirty workers are willing to work at the going wage but cannot obtain a job.

check.prompt: Does excess labor supply guarantee an immediate wage cut in this model?
check.answer: No. Firms may lose effort or incur higher turnover if they cut wages.

concepts.title: Effort responds to pay
concepts.explain: Workers may exert more effort when pay improves because they feel well treated or fear losing a valuable job. The effort curve relates real pay w to effort e(w), often drawn S-shaped.
concepts.formula: Effective labor = e(w)N
steps: Separate the number of workers from effort per worker.
Compare how effort responds to different wage levels.
Translate effective labor into production.
concepts.increase: A wage rise can increase effort and reduce turnover. The proportional effort increase may be large at intermediate wages.
concepts.decrease: A wage cut can reduce effort or increase shirking, so a lower wage per worker need not mean a lower cost per effective unit.
concepts.edge: Effort need not rise proportionately with wages everywhere. Diminishing incentive gains at high wages are central to an interior efficiency wage.
concepts.example: At w = 8 and e = 2, cost per effective unit is 4. At w = 10 and e = 3, it is 3.33, despite higher pay.

check.prompt: Why compare effective labor rather than worker counts alone?
check.answer: Different wages can buy different amounts of effort per worker.

concepts.title: Minimizing cost per effective worker
concepts.explain: The firm chooses the wage that minimizes w/e(w), equivalently maximizes e(w)/w. Graphically it is the point where a ray from the origin is tangent to the effort curve.
concepts.formula: min w/e(w); interior condition w e′(w) = e(w)
steps: Compute effort per dollar at candidate wages.
Choose the highest ratio or the tangency point.
Then choose employment given that wage and effort.
concepts.increase: Below an interior optimum, a small wage increase is worthwhile if effort rises by a greater percentage than pay.
concepts.decrease: Above the optimum, a small wage reduction is worthwhile if pay falls proportionately more than effort.
concepts.edge: The derivative condition needs an interior optimum and the appropriate curvature. It is not enough to pick any stationary point.
concepts.example: If e/w is 0.25 at w = 8, 0.30 at w = 10 and 0.28 at w = 12, wage 10 is best among those three.

check.prompt: At the interior efficiency wage, what is the elasticity of effort with respect to wages?
check.answer: One. The marginal percentage gain in effort equals the percentage increase in wage cost.

concepts.title: Efficiency wages and potential output
concepts.explain: In the lecture Keynesian setup, the efficiency wage and labor demand determine full-employment employment. A labor-supply shift by itself does not change that employment if supply remains sufficient.
concepts.formula: N* = Nᵈ(w_eff); Y* = A F(e(w_eff)N*, K). Fixed effort can be absorbed into productivity.
steps: Hold the effort relationship and efficiency wage fixed.
Read employment from labor demand.
Use production to determine potential output.
concepts.increase: More labor supply can increase unemployment without increasing Y* in this setup. Higher productivity can shift labor demand and raise Y*.
concepts.decrease: Less labor supply can reduce excess supply without changing Y*, until labor supply becomes a binding limit. Lower productivity can reduce Y*.
concepts.edge: This is why a fiscal wealth effect that shifts labor supply does not shift FE here. Do not import the Classical labor-market response.
concepts.example: If firms want 80 workers at the efficiency wage, labor supply increasing from 100 to 110 leaves employment 80 and raises excess supply from 20 to 30.

check.prompt: Why can immigration leave FE unchanged in this particular model?
check.answer: When the efficiency wage and labor demand determine hiring, additional labor supply only enlarges the pool of available workers.

concepts.title: Monopolistic competition and markups
concepts.explain: A differentiated producer faces downward-sloping demand and chooses output where MR = MC, then obtains its price from demand. Because price exceeds marginal revenue, price can exceed marginal cost.
concepts.formula: MR = MC; P = (1+κ)MC for markup κ
steps: Find the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Read the selling price on demand.
Distinguish the chosen price from marginal revenue.
concepts.increase: A demand increase at a fixed price can lead the firm to supply more while P remains above MC.
concepts.decrease: A demand decrease can lead the firm to sell less at that fixed price.
concepts.edge: A competitive price taker has P = MR, unlike this firm. The fixed-price supply response is not unlimited when rising MC overtakes P.
concepts.example: If MC = 8 and markup κ = 0.25, P = 10. A small extra sale may remain profitable while its marginal cost stays below 10.

check.prompt: Why does MR lie below P for a downward-sloping demand curve?
check.answer: Selling an additional unit requires a price reduction that affects revenue on other units under uniform pricing.

concepts.title: Small adjustment costs can keep prices fixed
concepts.explain: Changing prices has administrative and customer-related costs. A profit-maximizing firm keeps its old price when the profit gain from resetting is smaller than the adjustment cost.
concepts.formula: Reset price if gain from adjustment > menu cost
steps: Find the optimal new price absent costs.
Compare the profit gain with the actual adjustment cost.
Choose whether to reset now.
concepts.increase: A larger shock can make the gain exceed the menu cost and induce a price change.
concepts.decrease: A smaller shock can leave the gain below the menu cost, so the price remains unchanged.
concepts.edge: Rational optimization does not imply frictionless instantaneous adjustment. Equal benefit and cost gives indifference in the simple rule.
concepts.example: Resetting would raise profit by 30 but costs 50. Keeping the current price is privately optimal even though it is not the frictionless optimum.

check.prompt: Must firms reset prices after every change in demand?
check.answer: No. They compare the benefit of resetting with its cost.

concepts.title: Monetary and fiscal policy with rigid prices
concepts.explain: Monetary expansion increases real balances and lowers r. Fiscal expansion raises goods demand and r. Both can raise short-run output, but their composition effects differ. With fixed FE, prices later restore potential output.
concepts.formula: Monetary expansion → r↓; fiscal expansion → r↑ in the standard short run
steps: Specify which curve shifts.
Trace interest-sensitive private spending.
Distinguish the short-run output effect from the long-run price response.
concepts.increase: More M raises short-run C and I through lower r. More G raises Y but crowds out part of private spending through higher r.
concepts.decrease: Less M reduces short-run C and I through higher r. Less G reduces Y but lower r supports private spending.
concepts.edge: Keynesian tax-cut stimulus here rejects Ricardian equivalence. Long-run neutrality for money does not mean fiscal policy leaves the spending composition unchanged.
concepts.example: If G rises 10 and Y rises 6 initially, private spending changes by −4. When Y returns to its original fixed potential, private spending is lower by 10.

check.prompt: Can two policies raise Y but move investment in opposite directions?
check.answer: Yes. A money expansion lowers r and supports I, while a G expansion raises r and crowds out some I.

concepts.title: Why stabilization is difficult
concepts.explain: Policy can offset demand fluctuations, but the current output gap, multiplier and future conditions are uncertain. Decisions and transmission take time. A policy suited to yesterday’s economy can destabilize tomorrow’s.
concepts.formula: Policy effect today depends on earlier decisions and variable transmission lags
steps: Diagnose the shock and estimate the gap.
Account for decision and implementation delays.
Judge the likely state when effects arrive.
concepts.increase: An expansion arriving after recovery can push demand above capacity and increase inflation.
concepts.decrease: A contraction arriving during weakening demand can deepen a recession.
concepts.edge: The lecture argues against fine tuning while allowing intervention in major recessions. This is a conditional recommendation, not guaranteed success.
concepts.example: If stimulus takes nine months to affect demand but the economy recovers in three, the timing may be excessive even if the initial diagnosis was correct.

check.prompt: Why is knowing the sign of a multiplier insufficient for successful stabilization?
check.answer: The size, timing and future state of the economy also matter.

concepts.title: Supply shocks and stagflation
concepts.explain: An adverse oil shock reduces productive capacity and can prompt affected firms to raise prices quickly. FE shifts left and the higher P reduces real balances, shifting LM up. Lower output and higher prices can occur together.
concepts.formula: Oil cost↑ → effective productivity↓ → FE left; P↑ → M/P↓ → LM up
steps: Separate the potential-output decline from the demand response.
Locate actual output relative to the new potential.
Evaluate policy against the resulting gap and inflation.
concepts.increase: Higher oil prices can reduce Y* and raise P. Expansionary demand policy may close a remaining negative gap but adds inflation pressure.
concepts.decrease: Lower oil prices can improve capacity and reduce price pressure. The exact short-run output gap still depends on demand and price responses.
concepts.edge: Lecture p45 explicitly says output below the new FE is not logically necessary. A fall in Y is not enough to identify the gap.
concepts.example: Before a shock Y* = 100. Afterwards Y* = 90 and actual Y = 92. Output fell, but the economy is 2 above its new potential, not in a negative output gap.

check.prompt: Can demand stimulus restore the productive capacity directly lost in the oil shock?
check.answer: No. It can affect demand relative to the new capacity, while the supply constraint remains.

lessons.title: Inflation, unemployment and expectations
lessons.subtitle: Use surprises, natural rates and history to interpret the tradeoff.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 9 - The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve.pdf

concepts.title: The expectations-augmented curve
concepts.explain: The stable relationship in the model is between unexpected inflation and cyclical unemployment. Expected inflation and the natural unemployment rate determine where the short-run curve lies.
concepts.formula: π = πᵉ − h(u−u*), h > 0
steps: Compute cyclical unemployment u−u*.
Multiply by −h.
Add expected inflation.
concepts.increase: If u rises above u*, actual inflation is below expected inflation.
concepts.decrease: If u falls below u*, actual inflation is above expected inflation.
concepts.edge: At u = u*, inflation equals expected inflation, which need not be zero.
concepts.example: With πᵉ = 3%, h = 0.5 and u−u* = 2 percentage points, π = 2%.

check.prompt: Does zero cyclical unemployment require zero actual inflation?
check.answer: No. It requires actual inflation equal to expected inflation.

concepts.title: Positive, negative and zero surprises
concepts.explain: The sign of actual inflation alone does not determine the output or unemployment gap. Compare actual inflation with what was expected.
concepts.formula: π−πᵉ = −h(u−u*)
steps: Subtract expected inflation from actual inflation.
Use the opposite sign for the cyclical unemployment gap.
Relate unemployment to output via Okun’s law.
concepts.increase: A positive inflation surprise implies u below u* and output above potential in the model.
concepts.decrease: A negative inflation surprise implies u above u* and output below potential.
concepts.edge: Inflation can be positive but below expectations. Deflation can be less severe than expected and hence be a positive surprise.
concepts.example: Actual inflation 2% with expected inflation 4% is a −2-point surprise. Actual inflation −1% with expected −3% is a +2-point surprise.

check.prompt: If actual inflation is 1% and expected inflation is 5%, is unemployment above or below its natural rate?
check.answer: Above, because inflation is lower than expected.

concepts.title: Expected inflation shifts the curve
concepts.explain: Holding the natural rate and slope fixed, higher expected inflation raises actual inflation at every unemployment rate. This is a shift of the short-run curve, not movement along it.
concepts.formula: At fixed u and u*, Δπ = Δπᵉ
steps: Freeze the unemployment gap.
Change expected inflation.
Translate the entire short-run curve vertically.
concepts.increase: Higher πᵉ shifts the curve up. Sustaining the same unemployment requires higher actual inflation.
concepts.decrease: Lower πᵉ shifts it down. The same unemployment can coexist with lower actual inflation.
concepts.edge: Anchored expectations mean πᵉ need not follow every recent inflation observation. The adjustment rule is an additional assumption.
concepts.example: If πᵉ rises from 2% to 4% with the gap unchanged, predicted actual inflation rises 2 percentage points.

check.prompt: Does an increase in actual inflation necessarily shift the curve?
check.answer: No. With πᵉ and u* fixed, it can be a movement along the existing curve.

concepts.title: A changing natural rate
concepts.explain: The natural rate reflects frictional and structural unemployment when output is at full employment. Changing labor-market matching or institutions can shift it independently of aggregate demand.
concepts.formula: At fixed πᵉ and h, a rise in u* shifts the curve right; LRPC at u = u*
steps: Identify the change in structural or frictional conditions.
Move the natural-rate position.
Recalculate the cyclical gap using the new u*.
concepts.increase: A higher natural rate shifts the short-run curve up/right and the long-run curve right.
concepts.decrease: A lower natural rate shifts the short-run curve down/left and the long-run curve left.
concepts.edge: A rise in actual u is not proof that u* rose. Demand weakness can raise only cyclical unemployment.
concepts.example: With actual u = 6%, changing u* from 4% to 5% reduces cyclical unemployment from 2 to 1 percentage point.

check.prompt: Why must the gap be recalculated after a structural change?
check.answer: The relevant benchmark u* has changed, so the same actual u represents a different cyclical condition.

concepts.title: Supply shocks and the shifting tradeoff
concepts.explain: A supply disturbance can raise inflation expectations and increase structural mismatch, raising the natural unemployment rate. Both effects shift the short-run Phillips curve upward/right.
concepts.formula: Supply shock → πᵉ↑ and/or u*↑ → SRPC up/right
steps: Identify the expectations effect.
Identify the job-matching or natural-rate effect.
Combine them without treating the shock as a movement along a fixed curve.
concepts.increase: An adverse energy shock can produce higher inflation and higher unemployment together.
concepts.decrease: A favorable supply improvement can reduce inflation pressure and improve employment conditions.
concepts.edge: The original inverse inflation–unemployment relation only holds with πᵉ and u* approximately fixed. Stagflation is not a contradiction of a shifting curve.
concepts.example: Energy-intensive sectors shrink while energy suppliers expand. Workers may not instantly match to new jobs, so natural unemployment can rise.

check.prompt: How can both inflation and unemployment rise?
check.answer: The short-run curve can shift up/right due to expectations or supply-side changes.

concepts.title: Deriving the curve from SRAS
concepts.explain: Rearrange the misperceptions SRAS, subtract last period’s log price and connect the output gap to unemployment with Okun’s law. This translates the same surprise mechanism into inflation–unemployment space.
concepts.formula: P = Pᵉ +(Y−Y*)/b; π = πᵉ +(Y−Y*)/b; (Y−Y*)/b = −h(u−u*)
steps: Interpret P as log price for the inflation transformation.
Subtract the same previous-period log price from actual and expected log prices.
Use Okun’s negative output-gap/unemployment-gap relation.
concepts.increase: A positive price surprise raises output and creates a positive inflation surprise with lower cyclical unemployment.
concepts.decrease: A negative price surprise lowers output and creates a negative inflation surprise with higher cyclical unemployment.
concepts.edge: Price levels and inflation rates have different units. The logarithmic interpretation or an explicit growth-rate approximation is needed, not simply relabeling P as π.
concepts.example: If log P exceeds expected log P by 0.02, inflation exceeds expected inflation by 0.02 when both use the same previous log price.

check.prompt: Why do SRAS and the Phillips curve slope in opposite directions?
check.answer: Higher output corresponds to lower unemployment through Okun’s law.

concepts.title: Anticipated and surprise policy
concepts.explain: An unexpected demand expansion moves the economy along a short-run Phillips curve. A fully anticipated policy adjusts expected inflation, shifting the curve and leaving unemployment at its natural rate in the misperceptions model.
concepts.formula: Surprise policy changes π−πᵉ; anticipated policy can change π and πᵉ together
steps: State whether the policy was anticipated.
Decide whether expectations stay fixed or change.
Distinguish movement along a curve from a shift.
concepts.increase: Unexpected expansion raises inflation and lowers unemployment temporarily. Anticipated higher money growth raises expected and actual inflation without a lasting employment gain.
concepts.decrease: Unexpected contraction lowers inflation and raises unemployment temporarily. Anticipated lower money growth lowers expected and actual inflation with u at u* in the model.
concepts.edge: The output response to credible anticipated policy differs in sticky-price models. Do not generalize the misperceptions neutrality result to every framework.
concepts.example: With h = 1, an unexpected 2-point inflation increase implies a 2-point fall in u relative to u*. If πᵉ rises by the same amount, the gap is zero.

check.prompt: Can permanently higher anticipated inflation permanently reduce unemployment below u* here?
check.answer: No. Expected inflation catches up and the short-run curve shifts.

concepts.title: The natural-rate hypothesis
concepts.explain: Demand disturbances alter output and unemployment temporarily, but after expectations and prices adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate. This produces a vertical long-run Phillips curve.
concepts.formula: Long run π = πᵉ and u = u*
steps: Allow expectations to catch up to actual inflation.
Set the surprise term to zero.
Locate unemployment at its natural rate.
concepts.increase: Permanently higher money growth produces higher long-run inflation, not permanently lower unemployment.
concepts.decrease: Permanently lower money growth produces lower long-run inflation, not permanently higher unemployment under the natural-rate hypothesis.
concepts.edge: The natural rate can change for structural reasons. Vertical does not mean the long-run curve is fixed forever.
concepts.example: An economy can have u = 5% with inflation 2% or 8% if expectations match actual inflation and u* = 5%.

check.prompt: What makes the long-run curve vertical?
check.answer: Inflation surprises disappear while unemployment is pinned to the natural rate.

concepts.title: The natural rate is estimated
concepts.explain: The natural rate is not observed directly. Different estimates and revisions can change the inferred output gap and therefore the policy recommendation.
concepts.formula: Estimated cyclical unemployment = observed u − estimated u*
steps: Observe actual unemployment.
Compare plausible estimates of the natural rate.
Assess whether the sign of the gap is robust.
concepts.increase: A higher estimate of u* makes a given actual unemployment rate look less recessionary or more overheated.
concepts.decrease: A lower estimate makes the same actual unemployment rate look more recessionary.
concepts.edge: A point estimate should not be treated as exact. A confidence interval can straddle actual unemployment and leave the sign uncertain.
concepts.example: If u = 6% and plausible u* spans 4.8% to 6.6%, the cyclical gap ranges from +1.2 to −0.6 percentage points.

check.prompt: Can an imprecise natural-rate estimate support certainty about the sign of the gap?
check.answer: Not when plausible values lie on both sides of observed unemployment.

concepts.title: History can change the natural rate
concepts.explain: Hysteresis means a temporary shock leaves a persistent effect after the shock has disappeared. Prolonged unemployment can erode skills, weaken attachment or change bargaining power, shifting the natural rate itself.
concepts.formula: Temporary demand loss → persistent change in u* and Y*
steps: Trace unemployment during the shock.
Identify a mechanism that survives after demand recovers.
Distinguish persistent structural damage from a temporary cyclical gap.
concepts.increase: A severe or prolonged recession can raise u* through skill loss, lost job-search attachment or insiders excluding outsiders.
concepts.decrease: Preventing prolonged unemployment or improving retraining and matching may reduce persistent damage. An aggressive-demand strategy to lower u* remains controversial.
concepts.edge: Hysteresis challenges the strong claim that every demand shock leaves long-run real outcomes unchanged. It is an alternative hypothesis, not an automatic result of the standard Phillips equation.
concepts.example: After layoffs, fewer insiders influence wage bargaining. They may favor higher wages that keep outsiders unemployed even after the initial demand shock ends.

check.prompt: What evidence would distinguish hysteresis from a purely temporary gap?
check.answer: Unemployment or the estimated natural rate remains persistently altered after the original disturbance has ended, with a plausible persistence mechanism.

questions.prompt: Two internally consistent models predict different output responses to the same demand shock. What should you inspect first?

choices.feedback: A shared shock sign does not force the same response under different assumptions.
Different price, wage or capacity assumptions can change the mechanism and prediction.
Magnitude alone cannot identify the applicable model.
More equations do not ensure the right assumptions.

choices.text: Whether one model contains any exogenous variables
choices.feedback: Both can legitimately contain exogenous variables.

questions.explanation: Different price, wage or capacity assumptions can change the mechanism and prediction.

questions.prompt: In c=10+0.6y, y is supplied to the model and c is calculated. Which classification is correct?

choices.text: Both exogenous because the equation is simple
choices.feedback: An equation can determine an endogenous variable even when simple.
y is income; the intercept 10 is the autonomous component.
The model solves c while taking y as given.
This reverses which variable is determined.

choices.text: Both endogenous because both are letters
choices.feedback: Notation does not determine classification.

questions.explanation: The model solves c while taking y as given.

questions.prompt: A wage is taken as given by one firm but is solved by labor-market clearing in a larger model. Which statement follows?

choices.text: The wage must be exogenous everywhere
choices.feedback: That is not a permanent property of the variable.

choices.text: The wage must be zero in the firm model
choices.feedback: Taking a value as given does not set it to zero.

choices.text: The wage is a stock in the larger model
choices.feedback: Being endogenous does not turn a price into a stock.

choices.text: A variable can be exogenous in one model and endogenous in another
choices.feedback: Classification depends on which relationships the model includes.

choices.text: The firm model is logically inconsistent
choices.feedback: A price-taking firm can take a market-determined price as given.

questions.explanation: Classification depends on which relationships the model includes.

questions.prompt: In C=20+0.7Y−2r, Y rises while 20 and r stay fixed. What changes?

choices.feedback: The autonomous component remains 20.
The coefficient 2 remains fixed.
A change in its income argument moves along the relationship.
Nothing sets the intercept to zero.
The response is 0.7 times the income change, not a change in the autonomous intercept.

questions.explanation: The response is 0.7 times the income change, not a change in the autonomous intercept.

questions.prompt: C=15+0.5Y−r. At Y=100 and r=4, confidence raises the intercept to 22. What is the consumption change?

choices.feedback: Only the intercept changes, from 15 to 22, so consumption rises by 7.
The MPC applies to income, not to an intercept change.
22 is the new intercept, not its change.
Y and r can stay fixed while autonomous consumption changes.
The higher intercept raises consumption.

questions.explanation: Only the intercept changes, from 15 to 22, so consumption rises by 7.

questions.prompt: A nominal wage is 180 and the output price is 6. What is the real wage?

choices.feedback: 180 is the nominal wage before price adjustment.
Divide the nominal wage by the price, 180/6=30.
Multiplying does not measure purchasing power.
Subtracting a price from a wage is not the conversion.
6 is the price level, not the real wage.

questions.explanation: Divide the nominal wage by the price, 180/6=30.

questions.prompt: Nominal wages rise 8% and prices rise 10%. What happens to real wages?

choices.feedback: −2% is the first-order approximation. The exact ratio 1.08/1.10−1 gives a real-wage decline of about 1.82%.
The two proportional increases differ.
The exact change is 1.08/1.10−1≈−0.01818.
Adding growth rates is not the real-wage calculation.
This ignores the price increase.

questions.explanation: The exact change is 1.08/1.10−1≈−0.01818.

questions.prompt: A household sees its nominal income and every relevant price double, with quantities and opportunities otherwise unchanged. Which conclusion fits the course assumption about real choices?

choices.feedback: Both income and prices doubled, so quantities are unchanged.

choices.text: Its real wage necessarily becomes zero
choices.feedback: A proportional rescaling does not erase the wage.

choices.text: It is necessarily twice as happy
choices.feedback: Identical real opportunities do not imply a utility doubling.
The real budget is unchanged when all nominal values scale equally.
Real income divides nominal income by prices.

questions.explanation: The real budget is unchanged when all nominal values scale equally.

questions.prompt: Which item is a stock?

choices.feedback: Investment over a year is a flow.
Saving per month is a flow.
The deficit over a year is a flow.
Production over a quarter is a flow.
Debt measured at a date is a stock.

questions.explanation: Debt measured at a date is a stock.

questions.prompt: A capital stock starts at 100. Gross investment is 12 and depreciation is 15. What is the ending capital stock?

choices.feedback: Net investment is 12−15=−3, so ending capital is 97.
This omits depreciation.
Depreciation removes capital rather than adding it.
The net investment sign is reversed.
Gross investment is a flow, not the ending stock.

questions.explanation: Net investment is 12−15=−3, so ending capital is 97.

questions.prompt: A person has assets of 150 and liabilities of 90. What is their net worth?

choices.feedback: The subtraction is reversed.
Net worth is assets less liabilities.
Adding liabilities treats debt as wealth.
This ignores debt.
Liabilities alone are not net worth.

questions.explanation: Net worth is assets less liabilities.

questions.prompt: Someone borrows 20 and keeps all proceeds as cash. Immediately, before spending or interest, how does net worth change?

choices.feedback: Assets and liabilities do not both add to net worth.
The initial net worth need not be negative.
Cash assets and debt liabilities both rise by 20.
This ignores the new liability.
This ignores the new cash asset.

questions.explanation: Cash assets and debt liabilities both rise by 20.

questions.prompt: A household starts with assets 200 and debt 80. During the year it earns 60, consumes 45, repays 10 of principal from its unconsumed income, holds the other 5 as cash, and experiences a 12 asset-price loss. What are saving and ending net worth?

choices.feedback: Debt repayment uses part of the 15 saving and must not be counted twice.
This omits the asset-price loss.
The 12 capital loss reduces wealth, not saving from current income.
Saving is 60−45=15. Paying debt is one use of that saving, not an extra expense or extra saving. Initial wealth 120 rises by 15 and falls by 12, ending at 123.
Principal repayment is not consumption; the 10 also raises net worth.

questions.explanation: Saving is 60−45=15. Paying debt is one use of that saving, not an extra expense or extra saving. Initial wealth 120 rises by 15 and falls by 12, ending at 123.

questions.prompt: On a labor-demand graph with the real wage vertical and employment horizontal, a lower real wage with unchanged technology produces what?

choices.feedback: A shift needs a change in a held-fixed determinant.
The wage change is not a demand shifter.

choices.text: No change in employment under diminishing MPN
choices.feedback: A lower wage increases desired hiring under diminishing MPN.

choices.text: A higher MPN at the new employment level
choices.feedback: More employment reduces MPN to the lower wage.

choices.text: A movement down and right along the curve
choices.feedback: The wage is an axis variable, so changing it moves along a fixed labor-demand curve.
